0.title: Faith That Works: The Letter of James
0.overview:
The message. James asks one searching question of everyone who says they believe: is your faith alive? Living faith does not stay hidden in the head. It holds steady in trials, honours the shabby visitor as much as the rich one, bridles the tongue, humbles itself before God, waits for the Lord’s coming and prays. Faith that does none of these things is not a weaker kind of faith; it is dead (2:17). With more than fifty commands in 108 verses, James is among the most practical books in the Bible, and among the most misunderstood. It is not a rival to the gospel of grace but its searching application: what does real faith look like on a Monday?

Background: the writer. The author calls himself simply “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). Only a James known to every church could write so briefly, and the natural identification is James the brother of the Lord (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19). During Jesus’ ministry he did not believe in him (John 7:5), but the risen Christ appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and he became a leader of the Jerusalem church, one of its “pillars” (Galatians 2:9; Acts 12:17). He led the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:13–21), whose letter opens with the same unusual greeting as this one (Acts 15:23). Josephus records that he was put to death by the high priest about AD 62. James son of Zebedee, killed about AD 44 (Acts 12:2), is unlikely, and James son of Alphaeus is barely known.

Did James really write it? Some scholars think not, pointing to its good Greek, its silence about James’s family tie to Jesus, and its slow acceptance in parts of the early church, where it was counted among the disputed books. But Greek was widely used in Galilee, and he may have had help with his style. A brother who calls himself only Jesus’ “servant” shows the humility we would expect of a man who once disbelieved. Its slow acceptance owed more to its brevity and Jewish address than to doubts about its contents, and its Jewish world, farming scenes and closeness to Jesus’ sayings fit early Palestine well. This commentary holds that James the Lord’s brother wrote it.

When, and to whom. It is addressed “To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” (1:1): Jewish believers living outside the land, perhaps some of those scattered after Stephen’s death (Acts 8:1; 11:19). They still met in what James calls, in Greek, their synagogue (2:2, “assembly”), and confessed that “God is one” (2:19), the creed of every Jew. The letter says nothing about the dispute over circumcising Gentiles, so it was probably written before the Jerusalem Council of AD 49, in the mid-40s, perhaps the earliest book of the New Testament. Some date it to the late 50s and read chapter 2 as answering a twisted form of Paul’s teaching, but the earlier date fits better.

Their world. Most were poor and under pressure. Rich landowners dragged them into court (2:6) and kept back the wages of the day labourers who mowed their fields (5:4), though the law required a hired man to be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). Traders planned their year’s profit as if tomorrow were theirs (4:13). The farmer waited on “the early and the late rains” (5:7), the autumn and spring rains on which every harvest depended.

Its roots. James echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount again and again: joy in trials (1:2; Matthew 5:11–12), asking and receiving (1:5; Matthew 7:7), mercy to the merciful (2:13; Matthew 5:7), treasure that rots (5:2–3; Matthew 6:19–20), a plain “yes” and “no” (5:12; Matthew 5:34–37). It stands in the line of Proverbs, with short sayings and vivid pictures: the wave of the sea, the mirror, the bit and the rudder, the forest fire, the morning mist. And it speaks with the fire of the prophets, above all in its woe to the rich (5:1–6).

How the letter makes its case. Chapter 1 is an overture, sounding the themes the letter develops: trials that produce steadfastness (1:2–12), temptation that comes from our own desire, never from God (1:13–18), and the word that gives new birth and must be done, not only heard (1:19–27). Chapter 2 forbids favouritism toward the rich (2:1–13) and then asks what real faith is (2:14–26). Chapter 3 turns to the tongue, small but able to set a forest ablaze (3:1–12), and to the wisdom from above, “first pure, then peaceable” (3:13–18). Chapter 4 traces quarrels to warring desires and friendship with the world, calls the proud to humble themselves before God, and warns against judging others and boasting about tomorrow. Chapter 5 pronounces woe on rich oppressors (5:1–6), then turns tenderly to the suffering church: be patient until the Lord comes (5:7–11), speak without oaths (5:12), pray in every condition, the elders for the sick (5:13–18), and bring the wanderer home (5:19–20). Throughout, the “double-minded” (1:8; 4:8), divided between God and the world, are set against the whole-hearted believer, “perfect and complete” (1:4).

James and Paul. Martin Luther famously called James “a right strawy epistle” compared with books such as Romans, Galatians and John’s Gospel. Fighting the Roman Catholic teaching that works earn merit before God, he read James as a rival to Paul, when the two belong together. Paul says Abraham was justified by faith (Romans 4); James says he was “justified by works” (2:21). They face different errors. Paul opposes adding works to faith as the ground of acceptance with God; James opposes a “faith” that is only agreement with true doctrine, which even the demons have (2:19). Paul speaks of God’s verdict that a sinner is righteous, received through faith alone; James speaks of that faith shown to be real, as Abraham’s faith, counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6), was “completed by his works” when he offered Isaac (2:22–23). Paul says faith alone justifies; James says the faith that justifies is never alone.

Where it leads: to Christ. James names Jesus only twice, but calls him “the Lord of glory” (2:1), the one whose “honorable name” his people bear (2:7). He is the Lord whose coming is near and the Judge “standing at the door” (5:8–9). The letter’s law is his: “the royal law” of love to neighbour (2:8), “the law of liberty” (1:25; 2:12). Its demands drive us back to him. No one can tame the tongue (3:8) or keep the whole law (2:10), but God “gives more grace” (4:6), and he “brought us forth by the word of truth” (1:18), the gospel of his Son. Only Christ has lived the life James describes perfectly, and only his life in us produces it.

For us. James will not let you rest in a Christianity of the head alone. Does your faith survive under pressure? Does it make you generous and fair to the overlooked? Does it bridle your tongue? Does it humble you? Does it make you pray? They are not about earning salvation but about whether what you call faith is real. James offers no second route to God; he describes what grace produces in those who have received it. That is the faith that works, and it is the only faith that is faith at all.

1.title: Tested and Proven: Trials, Wisdom, and the Word
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 is the letter’s overture, sounding nearly every theme James will develop (see the introduction). All that follows rests on its two great facts: God is at work in your trials, and he has given you new birth by his word.

The message. God is not against you in your trials but for you in them, finishing a work in you; he gives every good thing and never tempts you to sin. So trust him with a whole heart, not a divided one, and let the word he has planted in you show in what you do. A faith that only listens is not yet the real thing.

Why it was said. The readers were scattered Jewish believers, mostly poor and pressed by the rich and powerful (see the introduction). Pressure tempted them to read their troubles as a sign that God had turned cold, to blame him when they sinned, to answer injustice with quick anger, and, like every church, to mistake listening to the word for obeying it.

How the chapter makes its case. Trials rightly reckoned produce maturity (vv. 2–4); the wisdom to bear them is God’s to give, though not to the double-minded (vv. 5–8); the lowly are exalted and the rich will fade (vv. 9–11); the crown of life waits for those who endure (v. 12). Temptation is born of our own desire, while the unchanging Father gives only good, above all the new birth (vv. 13–18). That word must be heard humbly and done (vv. 19–25), and real religion is tested by the tongue, care for the defenceless and holiness (vv. 26–27). The key word is “perfect” or “complete” (vv. 4, 17, 25): not flawless, but whole. Its opposite is the double-minded man (v. 8).

Where it leads. To the one man who was never in two minds. Jesus learned obedience through suffering (Hebrews 5:8), met temptation with nothing in him for the bait to catch, and did every word he heard. He wore thorns so that those who love him might wear the crown of life, and he is the firstfruits from the dead, whose harvest we are. The brother who once thought him out of his mind now calls him “the Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 1) and himself his slave.

For us. When trouble comes, ask what God is building, not whether he has left. When you fall, stop blaming him and trace the desire to its root. And when you close your Bible, decide what you will do before you forget.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Trials, Wisdom, and the God Who Does Not Change
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your trials are not a sign that God has turned against you: he is using them to make you whole, and he gives only good. After the greeting (v. 1), James shows what testing produces (vv. 2–4), promises wisdom to all who ask with an undivided heart (vv. 5–8), sets poverty and wealth in God’s light (vv. 9–11) and holds out the crown of life (v. 12). Then he guards against the lie that God tempts: sin is born of our own desire (vv. 13–15), but every good gift, above all the new birth, comes down from the Father who never changes (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing and Tempting

God tests to prove and strengthen; he never tempts (see the note on vv. 13–15). Every good gift comes from the Father of lights, who does not change (see vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were scattered believers under real pressure.

Now: Counting trials joy is a judgment about what they produce (see the note on vv. 2–4).

verseByVerse.quote: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: Greetings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord’s own brother introduces himself only as Christ’s slave, and greets a scattered, struggling church by the noblest name in Israel’s history.

James. The author is James the Lord’s brother, who came to faith after the resurrection and led the Jerusalem church (see the introduction). Known as James the Just, he was remembered, Eusebius records from the second-century writer Hegesippus, for knees hardened like a camel’s from prayer. His letter is full of echoes of the Sermon on the Mount: the brother who once did not believe in Jesus (John 7:5) now writes in his words.

A servant. A slave, a man who belongs to someone else (doulos). Yet he was the Lord’s brother (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19). He had grown up in the same house and eaten at the same table for perhaps thirty years; in a church that prized connection with Jesus, that claim would have opened every door. He writes “slave”, and never mentions the relationship at all.

The Lord Jesus Christ. Once his brothers came to take him home, because people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). What changed is recorded in a single line: “Then he appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7). Now the doubting brother calls him Lord and Christ, and names him in the same breath as God. The man who knew Jesus longest from the outside came to know him last from the inside, and when he did, he bowed. That is what the risen Christ does with unbelief: he does not argue it away, he appears to it. The line belongs to a summary of the gospel Paul received and handed on, and Paul had met James himself (Galatians 1:19), so it is no later legend. The resurrection best accounts for a doubting brother who became a leader of the church and died for it.

The twelve tribes in the Dispersion. The Dispersion (scattering) was the name for Jews living outside the land of Israel; here it probably means Jewish Christians abroad, perhaps including those driven out after Stephen’s death (Acts 8:1; 11:19). James gives a scattered, frightened, poor collection of believers the most dignified name in Israel’s history. The church is God’s people scattered as pilgrims in the world (1 Peter 1:1), and nobody in it is a stray.

Greetings. The ordinary Greek salutation, literally “rejoice”, used as a letter greeting elsewhere in the New Testament only by a Roman officer (Acts 23:26) and by the Jerusalem council under this man’s presidency (Acts 15:23). It is a wordplay: the very next word in Greek is joy. James has barely said hello before he is talking about joy, to people under pressure.

What it does not mean. Addressing the twelve tribes does not make the letter only for ethnic Jews; it is Scripture for the whole church, and has fed Gentile believers for two thousand years.

Which James is this? James the son of Zebedee was killed around AD 44 (Acts 12:2), probably too early to have written this, and James the son of Alphaeus is barely known. Only the leader of the Jerusalem church could sign himself simply “James” and expect every church to know him (see the introduction).

Should James be in the Bible at all? Luther called it an epistle of straw in 1522, fearing it said too little of Christ and grace and taught justification by works. But he kept it in his Bible and preached from it, and his later followers and the whole Reformed tradition have received it gladly as Scripture. James does not deny justification by faith; he denies that a faith which produces nothing is the faith that justifies, as Paul does too (Galatians 5:6). Read as the Spirit’s word to comfortable believers, the straw turns out to be iron.

In everyday life. Most of us reach for something when we want to be taken seriously: the job title, the qualification, the person we know. James had the best connection in the history of the world and did not use it; belonging to Christ was enough, and it can be enough for you.

Where Christians differ: was James a full brother of Jesus? Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin all her life, so that the brothers of Jesus were cousins or children of Joseph by an earlier marriage; many Orthodox Christians hold the second view. This commentary’s view: the most natural reading of the New Testament is that James was a younger half-brother of Jesus, a son of Joseph and Mary born after him. Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (Matthew 1:25), and Jesus is called her firstborn (Luke 2:7). The Gospels name his brothers and mention sisters alongside Mary (Mark 6:3), and the Greek has good words for cousin which are never used of them. Others note that brother could be used loosely of relatives, and hold their views out of real honour for Mary; but perpetual virginity is not taught in Scripture. Nor does this lessen Mary’s honour. All generations call her blessed (Luke 1:48), and the best honour we can give her is to do what she said at Cana: whatever he tells you, do it (John 2:5).
verseByVerse.note: James was most likely the brother of Jesus, who came to faith after the resurrection and led the Jerusalem church. He was put to death about AD 62. “The Dispersion” means Jewish believers scattered outside the land of Israel. The letter echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trials are reason for joy, not because they are pleasant, but because God uses them to test faith, grow steadfastness and make his people mature.

Count it all joy, my brothers. Not “feel joy”. The verb is reckon, consider, an accounting word. James commands not an emotion, which nobody can produce on demand, but a judgment about what trials are, and a judgment can be made while you are still miserable. All joy means pure joy: not joy in the pain itself, but in what God is doing through it.

When you meet trials. When, not if. The verb means to fall into, as the man fell among robbers (Luke 10:30). You come round a corner into trials: the phone call, the diagnosis, the letter, the conversation that goes wrong.

Of various kinds. Many-coloured, like a woven cloth: poverty, persecution, illness, bereavement, the slow ache of a prayer not yet answered. Peter uses the same word of God’s varied grace (1 Peter 4:10): there is no shade of suffering without a matching shade of grace.

Testing produces steadfastness. The joy is not irrational but informed. Testing is the assayer’s term for the fire that proves metal genuine and refines it at once (1 Peter 1:7). It produces hypomonē: not passive resignation but the capacity to remain under a weight without collapsing. It cannot be learned from a book or handed over in answer to a prayer; it grows only while we are bearing the weight.

Its full effect. A warning is folded in. The process can be cut short, by escaping at any cost, by numbing it, by getting bitter, all of which end the discomfort and the work together. Do not walk out of the refiner’s shop while the metal is still in the fire.

Perfect and complete. Perfect (teleios) means finished, having reached its end, not sinless; complete means whole in every part. James is describing maturity, and the road to it runs through the thing you would most like to avoid.

The road the Son walked first. The maturity James describes is the likeness of a person: God’s purpose is that we be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). And Christ went this way first: “Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation” (Hebrews 5:8–9). He had no sin to be refined away; “made perfect” means fully fitted, through suffering, to be our Saviour. The maturity James promises is his likeness formed in us, by the same road.

What it does not mean. Not that we should pretend trials do not hurt, or seek out suffering. Jesus wept at a friend’s tomb and agonised in the garden (John 11:35; Mark 14:33–34); Christian joy is not the absence of tears but something underneath them. Nor must every hardship simply be accepted. If you can lawfully escape danger, get treatment, or leave an abusive situation, you should. Endurance is for what God does not remove, not a reason to stay where he has given you a way out.

Does this mean God sent my suffering? God rules over all things, including our trials, and nothing reaches his children except by his permission and for his purpose (Romans 8:28; Lamentations 3:37–38). But he does not delight in our pain, and many trials come through other people’s sin, which he hates. The comfort is not that every hard thing is good, but that none is wasted. The God who allowed Joseph to be sold by his brothers used it to save many lives (Genesis 50:20). You may not see the purpose this side of heaven, and you are not required to. You are invited to trust the one who does.

How can I count it joy when I am crushed or grieving or depressed? Remember the verb: reckoning, not feeling. You may weep every day this month and still be counting it joy, if in the tears you say: “Lord, I do not understand this, but I believe you are working, and I will not let go.” Many psalms do exactly that, beginning in darkness. If you are depressed, talk to your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; that is not a failure of faith. The joy James means is often quiet: a stubborn confidence that God is not finished, held with a trembling hand.

Is this not just positive thinking, or a Stoic stiff upper lip? No, and the difference is a Person. The Stoic said pain does not matter; positive thinking looks on the bright side. James says the pain is real and the tears are allowed, but the trial is in the hands of a Father who is using it to make you like his Son. Stoic calm rests on your own strength of mind, and breaks when that runs out. Christian joy rests on what God is doing, which is why the weak can have it too.

verseByVerse.quote: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever lacks the wisdom to live through a trial should ask God for it, and he will give it gladly, without reproach, to anyone who asks trusting him.

If any of you lacks wisdom. The connection is the point. Trials produce maturity, “lacking in nothing” (v. 4), but inside a trial you cannot see what it is doing or what to do next. So James goes on, “If any of you lacks”, with the same word. This is wisdom for the trial: how to act inside something you did not choose and cannot understand. Biblical wisdom is skill in living, seeing life from God’s point of view (Proverbs 2:6).

Let him ask God. That is the whole method. Not “work it out”, not “wait for clarity”: ask, and the present tense means keep asking. Solomon was offered anything and asked for an understanding mind to discern between good and evil, and God was pleased (1 Kings 3:9–12). He has not changed his mind about that prayer.

Without reproach. He gives generously (haplōs): singly, simply, without calculation, with an open hand and a whole heart. And without reproach, which is the tender one. He does not sigh, or remind you that you asked last month, or that you would not need to ask if you had listened the first time. He never tires of being asked. Generous, whole-hearted giving is not something God does occasionally. It is what he is.

And it will be given him. A flat promise, with no conditions about how clever you are, which James had first heard from his brother: “Ask, and it will be given to you”, and “how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:7–11). All such wisdom comes from one treasury: Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:30), and in him are hidden all its treasures (Colossians 2:3). To ask for wisdom in a trial is, at bottom, to ask to know Christ in it and to see it as he sees it. The answer may not be a plan. It will be more of him.

Ask in faith. This needs care, because it has wounded people. The doubting described is not the ache of a believer who struggles; the man who said “I believe; help my unbelief!” got what he asked for (Mark 9:24). The word means to be divided, at odds within oneself, debating whether to trust God or rely on something else. To ask in faith is to come trusting God’s character and promise, not your own certainty.

Like a wave of the sea. A wave has no fixed position; it goes wherever the wind pushes it. So does the man who wants God’s wisdom on Sunday and the world’s on Monday, who asks and then goes to arrange matters himself. He is not weak in faith but in two minds, and the next verses name it.

What it does not mean. Not that God will give whatever we ask if we only believe hard enough; the promise here is for wisdom, and in all our asking God answers according to his will (1 John 5:14). Faith is not a force we generate.

How does God actually give wisdom? Should I expect a voice or a sign? Ordinarily through his word, which is able to make you wise (2 Timothy 3:15), a mind renewed by it (Romans 12:2), the counsel of mature believers (Proverbs 15:22), and his providence opening and closing doors. Scripture is complete and sufficient, so we need no new revelations (Christians who believe God still guides by impressions or prophecy generally agree that any such sense must be tested by Scripture and can never add to it); the Spirit helps us understand and apply what he has already said. It often comes quietly: a passage that suddenly fits, a friend’s question, a growing clarity. Ask, read, seek counsel, then act on the best light you have, trusting God to correct you.

I asked for wisdom and I still do not know what to do. Sometimes wisdom is not a clear answer about the future but the grace to take the next right step: a lamp to your feet (Psalm 119:105), lighting one step at a time. If two paths are both lawful and both seem wise, you are free to choose, and God is not waiting to punish you for picking the wrong door. And sometimes the wisdom we lack is not what to do but how to bear what we cannot change, patiently, without bitterness. That is often the deepest answer to this prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord; he is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who asks God while keeping his own options open is divided at the centre, and he should not expect to receive anything from the Lord.

He is a double-minded man. Two-souled (dipsychos); so far as we can tell James coined the word, for it appears nowhere in Greek before this letter. He means a man with two genuine loyalties pulling in different directions, who prays sincerely and hedges sincerely. The contrast is with God, who gives simply (v. 5): the giver is undivided, and the asker is in two pieces.

The single eye. James learned the contrast from his brother. Jesus said that the healthy eye (literally the single eye, haplous, the word behind God’s generous giving in verse 5) fills the whole body with light, and that no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:22–24). A heart is made single not by straining to want one thing, but by finding the one Master worth all of it.

Unstable in all his ways. Not only in prayer; in all his ways. The word means restless, unsettled, and James uses it again of the tongue, a restless evil (3:8). A man divided at the centre is divided everywhere.

The disease of the whole letter. Double-mindedness is the root of everything James will confront: faith without works (2:14), blessing and cursing from one mouth (3:10), friendship with God and with the world (4:4). At 4:8 he gives the remedy: draw near to God, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. The whole letter is a call to be one person before God.

One man who was never in two minds. Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), and in the garden he prayed “Not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). We are not saved by our singleness of heart but by his, and his Spirit works in us to make our divided hearts single.

Why does such a man receive nothing? Not because God withholds out of pique. Rather, he is unable to receive: a man who asks for wisdom while intending to keep his options open has asked only for a second opinion, to weigh against the others. The searching question is not whether you doubt, but whether, before you prayed, you had already decided what you would do if the answer went the wrong way.

How do I know whether I am double-minded or simply weak? The weak believer wants God wholly and finds he cannot do it well; the double-minded man wants God partly and is content to keep it so. The weak believer grieves over his divided heart; the double-minded man has made his peace with it. So ask: is there an area where I have quietly decided God will not have the final word? Money, a relationship, my reputation, a habit? If you find one and it troubles you, that trouble is the Spirit’s work, the first sign of a heart being made whole.

Can a divided heart be made whole? Yes, and God does it. David prayed, “Unite my heart to fear your name” (Psalm 86:11), and God promised his people one heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 11:19). Pray David’s prayer, then give God the one area you are holding back in some concrete act this week. A heart is unified the way a divided kingdom is, by surrendering one province at a time to the rightful King.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. So also will the rich man fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ the poor believer is lifted high and the rich believer is brought low, so each should boast in what God has done, because wealth fades like a wild flower in the heat.

The lowly brother. James turns to money, and he will keep coming back to it. Lowly means of low status, and among these scattered believers it often meant genuinely poor. He is to boast in his high position: not in his poverty, nor only in a reward to come, but in what he already is, a child of God and an heir of the kingdom (2:5). His social position is the least true thing about him.

The rich in his humiliation. The two halves mirror each other, each saying the opposite of what the world says. The rich believer is to boast in being brought low: in discovering that his money buys nothing where it counts, that he came to God with empty hands, a sinner saved by grace on the same level as the poorest member of his church. That is a harder boast, and the only one available to him. God has always reversed the world’s rankings: “he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52).

Like a flower of the grass. The image is from Isaiah 40:6–8, which his readers knew by heart: all flesh is grass, the grass withers, the flower fades.

In the midst of his pursuits. Journeys, business trips. Not afterwards, when he can look back, but in the middle, with the plans half-made and the diary full, like the man in the Lord’s parable who had just decided to build bigger barns and was told, “This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:16–21). Wealth does not protect from death. It only gives a man more to leave behind.

Both boasts meet at the cross. Both believers are joined to a Saviour who went down before he went up. Christ emptied himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross; therefore God has highly exalted him (Philippians 2:7–9). The Lord of glory was brought lower than any refugee: born in a borrowed place, buried in a borrowed tomb, stripped even of his clothes. The lowly believer’s exaltation is his: God has raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6). The rich believer’s humiliation is his too: to kneel at the same cross with the same empty hands. In Christ every member of the church kneels on the same floor and is seated on the same throne.

What it does not mean. Not that wealth is sinful: Abraham and Job were rich and loved God. But wealth is temporary and gives no standing before him.

Who counts as rich today? Most of us reading this. Food for tomorrow, a roof, a choice of what to wear, some savings or a pension: by any historical or global measure, that is rich. James would read this to us, not to billionaires. The aim is not guilt but freedom: to hold what you have loosely, to give generously (1 Timothy 6:17–19), and to boast not in what you own but in being a beggar made an heir.

I am poor, and I am ashamed of it. What does this say to me? That your poverty is real but is not the truest thing about you. In God’s house there is no second class. You are a son or daughter of the King, and your inheritance cannot be repossessed (1 Peter 1:4). Hold your head up in church. And if you are in real need, it is not shameful to let your brothers and sisters help; the early church shared so that no one among them was needy (Acts 4:34), and that is still how a church is meant to work.

In everyday life. Read last month’s bank statement as a diary, because it is one: what does it say you love? Then do one thing that loosens money’s grip, gladly, because your riches are in Christ: give something away quietly, or cancel something you do not need.

Where Christians differ: is the rich man in verse 10 a believer? Some think “brother” carries over, so James is telling rich Christians to glory in their humbling. Others note that the rich in this letter are always outsiders and oppressors (2:6–7; 5:1–6), and read the line as bitter irony: let the rich man boast in the only thing coming to him, his destruction. Careful interpreters hold both. The first fits the grammar a little better and speaks to wealthy church members; the second fits the rest of the letter. Either way the lesson is the same: money is a flower, and whoever builds his life on it builds on something that will be brown by evening.

parallels.desc: The grass withers, the flower fades

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who keeps trusting God through trial is blessed, because when the test is over God will give him the crown of life promised to those who love him; that is why trials can be counted joy (v. 2).

Blessed. The word of the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12): happy, approved by God. “Remains steadfast” is the verb form of the steadfastness of verse 3.

When he has stood the test. The assayer’s word again, now as a verdict rather than a process. The metal has been through the fire and passed; the trial’s purpose was reached.

The crown of life. Usually the victor’s wreath at the games rather than a royal diadem (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4; Revelation 2:10). The phrase almost certainly means the crown which is life: not a decoration on top of eternal life, but eternal life itself as the prize.

Promised to those who love him. Two clauses keep this from being a wage. God has promised it, so it rests on a promise, not on the quality of the endurance. And it is promised to those who love him, not to those who endure impressively. The man described is not a stoic with unusual grit; he loves God, and steadfastness is what love looks like under weight.

The Lord’s own beatitude. James is repeating his brother: “the one who endures to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22), with the very verb used here. And the life that is the crown is not a prize handed out beside Christ, who is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25): to receive the crown of life is to receive him.

He wore the crown of thorns. Jesus was crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:9). Soldiers twisted thorns into a wreath and pressed it on his head as a joke, and God made the joke the truth: the King of glory was crowned there, in our place, under our curse. He wore the crown of thorns so that we could wear the crown of life, and he will set it on every head that loved him, however bruised.

A verse facing two ways. It closes the passage on trials, and its word for trial also means temptation, which is where James turns next. The hard circumstance God uses to prove our faith, our own desire can use to draw us into sin, so we need to know which is at work.

What if I did not endure well? I gave in, or grew bitter, or nearly walked away. Then hear the gospel first: the crown rests on God’s promise, not on your performance. Peter denied Christ three times in one night and was restored by Jesus beside a fire on the beach (John 21:15–19). Endurance in Scripture is not a perfect record but a faith that keeps getting up and coming back. If you still want Christ, you have not fallen away; you have stumbled, and the God who began a good work in you will finish it. Confess what went wrong, receive his forgiveness, and take the next step.

Are there different crowns for different Christians? The New Testament speaks of crowns of life, of righteousness and of glory (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4): not separate prizes for an elite but ways of describing the one gift every believer receives, eternal life with Christ, the righteousness he gives, the glory he shares. Faithful service will be rewarded (1 Corinthians 3:12–15), but no believer is outside the joy, and the elders in Revelation cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). The crowns end up at his feet.

In everyday life. Someone in your church is under a long trial: an illness, a hard marriage, a disabled child, a slow grief. Endurance is often lonely. Send them a message today, or visit, and tell them you see what they are carrying.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one say when he is tempted, “I am being tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pull to sin comes from our own desire, never from God, and desire left to grow gives birth to sin and finally to death.

Tempted by God. The same Greek word now shifts from testing to tempting: an inner pull towards sin. Somebody was saying it, or James would not forbid it, and the excuse is perennial: he made me this way; he put the opportunity in front of me. The first man said it within minutes of the first sin: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12). Not simply “the woman”, but “the woman whom you gave”.

God cannot be tempted. The answer comes in two absolute parts. God is untemptable: there is nothing in him for evil to appeal to, no foothold, no answering appetite. He is light in whom is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5).

He himself tempts no one. Yet God does test: he tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1), and James has just spent eleven verses saying trials do good work. The difference is the aim: a test is meant to prove and strengthen; a temptation, to destroy. One circumstance can be both at once, depending on who is using it for what. Joseph’s brothers meant it for evil; God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20).

Lured and enticed. Then James names the real source, closer to home. Both verbs come from hunting and fishing: lured is drawn out of cover; enticed comes from the word for bait. A fish is drawn from under the rock by something that looks like food, with the hook hidden inside. And the desire is “his own”. The source is not the circumstance, nor even the devil, whom James does not mention here. The devil does tempt (Matthew 4:1–11), but he can only dangle the bait. The bait works because of what is already in the fish.

Desire gives birth to sin. The picture changes to conception and birth. Desire, welcomed by the will, conceives and gives birth to sin, the act; sin grows to full term and delivers death (Romans 6:23): a terrible genealogy. Each stage looks manageable: a desire is not yet a sin, and a sin is small. James lays the whole line out in one sentence so that you can see the end from the beginning, the one thing desire never lets you do. The bait never shows you the hook, and the first step never shows you the grave.

The one the bait could not catch. James’s analysis has one exception, and the Gospels show him in the desert. Jesus was truly tempted: hungry and alone, he was offered bread, safety and the kingdoms of the world (Matthew 4:1–11). But the hook found nothing to catch on. He felt the full pull of temptation, more than we ever do, because he never gave in and so never felt it slacken. There was no sinful desire in him for the bait to draw out: “the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me” (John 14:30). Where the first Adam, in a garden full of food, blamed “the woman whom you gave”, the last Adam, starving in a wilderness, answered every lie with “It is written”, and blamed no one. The genealogy of desire, sin and death was reversed in him: he took our death, and gives us his life.

Then why does the Lord’s Prayer say lead us not into temptation? God brings his people into trials, but never to make them sin. In that prayer (Matthew 6:13) we ask to be kept from trials that would overwhelm us, and delivered from the evil one when they come. It is the prayer of someone who does not trust himself, exactly the posture James wants.

Is being tempted itself a sin? No. Our Lord was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Sin begins when the desire is welcomed and cherished, when it conceives (v. 15), and a temptation resisted is a victory, not a failure. Many sensitive Christians are tormented by thoughts they hate. The uninvited thought is the bait dangled; it becomes sin when you take it in, turn it over and want it. The very fact that you hate it shows whose side you are on.

So what do I actually do in the moment of temptation? Name it honestly: this is my desire, not God’s plan. Look past the bait to the hook and tell yourself where this leads. Flee if you can (2 Timothy 2:22); Joseph left his cloak and ran. Pray, briefly and at once, for he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). Fill the empty space with something good, and tell a trusted friend afterwards, since secrecy is the womb where desire conceives. And remember: God is faithful; he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

In everyday life. Trace the genealogy of your most frequent temptation. Where does the desire usually begin: tiredness, loneliness, a particular screen, person or hour of the night? That is where the battle is won or lost, long before the act. And stop saying, even silently, that it is not really your fault. Taking the blame is the beginning of freedom, because the blame you own is the blame Christ has already carried, and those who walk by the Spirit will not gratify the desires of the flesh (Galatians 5:16).

Where Christians differ: if God is sovereign over all things, is he the author of sin? Some object that the Reformed view of God’s sovereignty makes God responsible for evil. This commentary’s view: God is sovereign over all things, including the sinful acts of human beings, which he permits and overrules for his good purposes (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Yet he is never the author of sin, never tempts anyone, and never approves of evil (Westminster Confession 5.4; 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.4). Sin arises from the creature’s own desires. Scripture teaches both God’s sovereignty and human responsibility, and both must be held even when we cannot explain how they fit. The cross is the proof: the most wicked act in history was planned by God for the salvation of the world, and the men who did it were guilty of it.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “cannot be tempted” (apeirastos) occurs only here in the New Testament and is rare elsewhere. It most likely means “untemptable”, as the ESV has it, but it could mean “without experience of evil”, and a few take it as “ought not to be put to the test”. The first fits best with “he himself tempts no one”, and on any reading nothing in God answers to evil.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is never behind our temptation: everything good comes down from him, he never changes, and his best gift is the new birth he gave us by his word.

Every good gift. Do not be deceived: the lie that God set you up is no harmless mistake, and James answers it by describing what God is like. The traffic runs one way, and nothing bad comes down that road: if it is good, it came from there; if it came from there, it is good. In Greek the line has a poetic rhythm, almost a hexameter, and may be a saying James is quoting. “Good gift” stresses the giving; “perfect gift”, the thing given, complete. God gives well, and what he gives is whole.

The Father of lights. The maker of sun, moon and stars (Genesis 1:14–18; Psalm 136:7–9), a title chosen for what follows, because everybody knows that heavenly lights change. Sun, moon and shadows shift all day long.

No shadow due to change. The shadow cast by turning, as it moves round a sundial or the moon passes through its phases. The Father who made the changing lights does not himself change (Malachi 3:6; Hebrews 13:8): no season in him, no eclipse, no angle from which he looks different. This is God’s immutability.

The light does not flicker. In a trial we rarely doubt that God exists; we suspect that he has gone cool, favourable last year and not now. The light does not flicker. Your circumstances turn like the sky; the one who loves you does not.

He brought us forth. The supreme instance of the good gift. “Of his own will”: God’s sovereign choice. “Brought forth” is a birth word, deliberately answering verse 15, where sin, full-grown, brought forth death with the same verb. Two pregnancies, two deliveries, three verses apart: sin gives birth to death; God gives birth to life. This is regeneration, the new birth (John 1:13; 3:3–8; 1 Peter 1:3, 23).

By the word of truth. The gospel (Ephesians 1:13; Colossians 1:5). The new birth begins with God’s will, and he uses his word to do it (1 Peter 1:23). No one is born again without hearing of Christ, and no one born again can take the credit, because no one has ever caused his own birth. Before you wanted him, he willed you; before you could speak, he spoke his word of truth into your death, and you lived.

Firstfruits. Harvest language (aparchē): the first sheaf offered to God, both a real portion and a pledge that the whole harvest is his (Leviticus 23:10; see Firstfruits). These scattered believers are the opening instalment of a renewed creation; the whole groaning creation will follow (Romans 8:19–23).

Firstfruits of the risen firstfruits. The harvest began on a particular morning. Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). The first sheaf of the new creation was the body that came out of the tomb, and the word of truth by which God brings us forth is the news that Christ died for our sins and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). To be born again is to be joined to him, born again to a living hope through his resurrection (1 Peter 1:3); every believer is a sheaf from the field whose first sheaf was Christ.

What it does not mean. “Of his own will he brought us forth” does not make our response unreal: we truly believe and truly repent. But the new birth originates in God’s will, not our decision (John 1:13), and it comes before faith and produces it. You did not come alive by believing; you believed because God had already made you alive, as Lazarus walked out of the tomb only because the voice of Jesus had first given him life (John 11:43–44; Ephesians 2:4–5). Christians in the Arminian tradition, who hold that God’s grace enables every hearer to believe and that the new birth follows faith, read verses like this differently, and they too give God the glory for their salvation; this commentary holds the Reformed order because Scripture traces the new birth to God’s will before ours.

If God never changes, why does the Bible say he relented? When Scripture says God relented (Jonah 3:10), it describes his dealings from our side: his settled character is to punish the unrepentant and spare the repentant, so when people turn, his response turns with them. His purposes and character do not change, which is exactly why his responses are reliable, and why prayer is worth praying: not to a God who might be in a different mood today, but to one whose promises do not shift.

Does every good gift include good things unbelievers enjoy? Yes. Every sunrise, harvest, friendship, piece of music, act of healing and moment of laughter comes down from the Father of lights, whoever enjoys it. This is common grace: “he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45). The tragedy of the unbeliever is not that he receives no gifts but that he never thanks the Giver (Romans 1:21). The joy of the believer is to trace every good thing back up the road it came down.

In everyday life. If you are a believer, remember that you did not bring about your own new birth, so you cannot undo it on a bad day either.

Uncertain wording. “Variation or shadow due to change” uses rare words that sound almost technical, perhaps borrowed from talk of the heavenly bodies, and the exact picture is uncertain: the turning of sun and stars, the shifting shadow they cast, or simply any change at all. The meaning of the whole is not in doubt: unlike the lights he made, God never alters, dims or turns.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word that gave you new birth must be received humbly and done, because hearing alone deceives. Hearing it well means being quick to listen and slow to anger (vv. 19–20) and stripping off the sin that blocks the ears (v. 21). Hearing without doing is like studying your face in a mirror and forgetting it at once (vv. 22–24), but the one who stays bent over the law of liberty and acts is blessed (v. 25). James ends with three tests of real religion: the tongue, care for the defenceless and a life unstained by the world (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mirror

Hearing without doing is self-deception (see v. 22). The blessed man looks into the perfect law of liberty, stays there, and acts (see the note on v. 25).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Orphans and widows were the people with no one to speak for them (see vv. 26–27).

Now: Pure religion still means turning up for the helpless and keeping unstained from the world (see the note on vv. 26–27).

verseByVerse.quote: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who have received God’s word must listen eagerly, speak carefully and be slow to anger, because human anger never produces the righteous life God wants.

Not conversational tips. Set between the word of truth (v. 18) and the implanted word (v. 21), these commands first concern how to receive Scripture, and then, since one posture governs both, how to treat each other. The man who listens to God properly will begin to listen to people properly, and the man who interrupts God will interrupt everybody.

Quick to hear. Eager, leaning in, ready, the opposite of the man who already knows: towards God’s word above all, but also towards others, hearing the whole sentence, the whole story, the thing behind the thing.

Slow to speak. Not a call to silence; James preaches, and his letter is full of words. It is about order and speed (Proverbs 10:19; 17:27–28). A word that comes out too fast has not been weighed, and among pressured and frightened people the quick word was doing damage.

Slow to anger. Not “never angry”. “Slow” allows that some things ought to produce anger, and makes arriving there quickly the fault. God himself is slow to anger (Exodus 34:6), and his children are to be like him.

The anger of man. Produce means work out, accomplish; the righteousness of God is the righteous life God requires. That is a hard word for people angry about something genuine. Many of these readers were poor, some cheated by employers (5:4), and James thinks that scandalous. He does not say their anger is unjustified. He says it will not produce what it is aiming at.

One sequence. Slow to hear and quick to speak becomes quick to anger: the sequence begins with how you listen. Most quarrels are lost at the first stage, when one person stopped hearing and started preparing his reply.

The ear that was opened every morning. This order was once lived without a break. Isaiah’s Servant says that the Lord has given him the tongue of those who are taught, to sustain the weary with a word, and that morning by morning he awakens his ear to hear (Isaiah 50:4). And when he was reviled, the one with every right to anger was like a lamb led to the slaughter, and did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7; 1 Peter 2:23). Quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger: before it was a command to us, it was the life of the one who obeyed in our place.

Why does anger feel like virtue? In our public life anger has become the proof of sincerity, and the angriest voice wins the room. The Roman Stoic Seneca went the other way, urging in a whole treatise that anger, a brief madness, be rooted out altogether. James is more searching than either: he asks what anger produces, and answers that it does not produce the righteousness it is shouting for. Underneath most quick anger lies something we feel we must have, respect, control, being right, and someone standing in its way (4:1–2). That is why it burns so hot: it is defending a god. The gospel cools it at the root. God’s own anger at sin, which had every right to be quick, was patient with us for centuries and then fell on his Son. Those who know that can afford to be slow, and to leave judgment in better hands (Romans 12:19).

What it does not mean. Not that all anger is forbidden: “be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26), and Jesus looked around at the Pharisees with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). But human anger is usually mixed with pride and self-interest, and it must not be quick.

How do I become quick to hear? Start with God, where the posture is learned: open his word before the news or your messages, and ask what it says before deciding what you think of it. Then carry the posture into conversation. Let people finish their sentences, and notice the moment you start preparing your reply. Ask one more question than you normally would. Before you disagree, say back what you heard. Listen for the thing behind the thing: the tiredness in the voice, the fear under the complaint. This is being listened to by God, passed on: “Because he inclined his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live” (Psalm 116:2). Our high priest sympathises with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15) and has heard every one of our clumsy prayers to the end; people heard that patiently learn to hear others.

Does this mean I should stay quiet when I am being wronged or abused? No. Slow to anger is not a command to accept abuse or keep quiet about wrongdoing. Scripture commands us to defend the weak and expose deeds of darkness (Psalm 82:3–4; Ephesians 5:11). If you or anyone else is being harmed, speak up, get help, and if a crime is involved, go to the authorities. What James forbids is the hot, quick, self-righteous anger that lashes out and makes things worse. Righteous action is often calm, deliberate and firm; justice is better served by a clear head than a burning one.

How do I become slow to anger when it rises so fast? Begin with the first command, quick to hear: most anger is fed by assuming the worst, so ask, “What did you mean by that?” Give it time: a walk, a night’s sleep, an unsent email. Bring it to God before you bring it to the person (Psalm 4:4). And remember how slow God has been with you; nothing cools anger like that.

In everyday life. Online is where this rule matters most: read the post twice, wait an hour, and ask whether your reply will build anything.

Uncertain wording. “Know this, my beloved brothers”: the Greek verb can be a statement (“you know this”) or a command (“take note of this”). Most translations, like the ESV, take it as a command; either way James points his readers back to what they know about the word (v. 18) before telling them how to receive it.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “wherefore” here instead; the earliest have “know this”.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strip off the sin that blocks your ears, and humbly welcome the word God has planted in you, because that word has power to save.

Put away all filthiness. Put away is the verb for taking off a garment (Colossians 3:8). Filthiness is moral dirt, and a related word was used in medical writing of earwax, which blocks hearing. Whether or not James intended the pun, sin does block our ears to God’s word, and no one can be quick to hear with his ears stopped.

Rampant wickedness. An overflow of malice, evil grown past its bounds, which must be cut back before anything else can grow: the excess of evil that remains even in believers.

Receive with meekness. Take off, and take in: you cannot do the second while wearing the first. Receive means welcome, as you would a guest. Meekness is not weakness but strength that has stopped fighting back, the opposite of the anger of verse 20. Towards Scripture it means coming without a case to argue: not sitting in judgment on the text or sifting it for what confirms you, but letting it have the last word.

The implanted word. Planted in, rooted (emphytos, sometimes rendered engrafted). The word is not merely heard from outside; it was planted in them at their new birth (v. 18), and their task is to let it grow, not to fetch it.

Able to save your souls. Not merely to inform or improve, but to save: the final salvation of the whole person (5:20; 1 Peter 1:9). James is often accused of teaching mere good behaviour, yet he rests every command that follows on something God has planted, which does the saving.

Planted by a covenant sealed in blood. The word could be planted in these hearts only because of a table and a cross. The promise behind it, “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), is the new covenant, and on the night he was betrayed Jesus said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The implanted word is not self-help absorbed by effort but a gift his death bought and his Spirit sows.

What it does not mean. Not that believers are not yet saved; they have been born again (v. 18). But salvation has past, present and future aspects: we have been saved from sin’s penalty, are being saved from its power, and will be saved from its presence. The word keeps working to the end.

What does meekness toward Scripture look like when I find a passage hard or disagree with it? It means assuming that if you and the Bible conflict, you are the one who needs to move. Read the hard passage carefully, in context, asking what it actually says, not what you fear it says; seek help from good teachers; bring your questions to God honestly, as the psalmists did. But do not edit Scripture to fit your preferences. Meekness is not pretending to have no questions, but bringing them to the word as a pupil, not a judge.

In everyday life. A sin you are holding onto will make every sermon sound like someone else’s problem. Before you read, pray, “Speak, LORD, for your servant hears”; then read until something cuts against you, and stay there.

Uncertain wording. “Rampant wickedness” is literally “abundance (or surplus) of evil”. It may mean the wickedness that abounds all around, the malice that overflows from the heart, or, as some older translators took it, the remainder of evil still left in believers. On any reading, whatever evil remains is to be stripped off like a soiled garment.

verseByVerse.quote: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearing God’s word is not enough: it must be done, and the person who only listens is fooling himself. This is the thesis of the whole letter, and everything to chapter 5 applies it.

But be doers of the word. Doer (poiētēs, from which comes poet, a maker) is a noun: it describes what a person is, not one thing he once did. Receiving the word (v. 21) must lead to doing it, and the doing grows out of a gift: the Father brought us forth by this same word of truth (v. 18), and the word that gave us life goes on working in those who obey it.

And not hearers only. James does not disparage hearing; he has just commanded it. The problem is the word only. Hearers are an audience. The man in view does not refuse Scripture; he attends.

Deceiving yourselves. To reason falsely, to talk yourself into a wrong conclusion. This is not hypocrisy, which deceives others. It is a man doing the sum wrong about himself and believing the answer, which is why it is so dangerous: a hypocrite knows, and this man does not. He has heard the word, felt its force, agreed with it warmly, and counted his agreeing as doing.

A peculiarly religious danger. The more sermons a person hears, the more familiar the sensation of being moved, and the easier it is to mistake for change. It can even become a quiet way of trusting ourselves: our seriousness about the Bible, our notes and our attendance start to feel like what makes us right with God, when the word we hear keeps pointing us away from ourselves to Christ.

These words of mine. James is restating how his brother ended the Sermon on the Mount: everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock (Matthew 7:24–27). Doing them does not earn a place with him. It is building on him.

The Doer is making doers. There has been one perfect doer of the word. Jesus did not only hear his Father: “My food,” he said, “is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). Every word he heard, he did, all the way to the cross, with never a gap between hearing and doing, not even in Gethsemane. We never obey like that, but his unbroken obedience is counted as ours, the righteousness in which his people stand, and it is also the life his Spirit is reproducing in them, slowly, word by word. The Doer is making doers, and he will finish what he has begun.

Does James contradict Paul here? No. Paul also says it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God (Romans 2:13), and that faith works through love (Galatians 5:6). Both teach that we are saved by grace through faith alone, and that the faith which saves is never alone; it bears fruit (Ephesians 2:8–10). Paul fights those who add works to faith as the ground of salvation; James fights those who think faith can be real without works. They stand back to back, facing different enemies. James makes the case at length in 2:14–26, where Abraham and Rahab show that the faith which justifies is a living, working faith.

I have been a hearer for years. Where do I even start? Not with a programme but with one thing. Take the clearest thing God has said to you recently, the thing you already know you should do, and do it this week. Most of us are not short of information; we are carrying a backlog of obedience. Start at the front of the queue. And do not despair over the years: the God who planted the word is patient, and a hearer who begins to do is exactly what this verse is for.

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hearer who does not act is like a man who studies his face in a mirror and forgets it the moment he walks away.

A mirror. He does not glance: the verb means to look intently, to study. The hearer in this picture is engaged in the moment. His natural face is literally the face of his birth, what he was born with and cannot alter by wishing.

At once forgets. The failure lies in what comes next, told in three verbs. He looked, genuinely. He left. And by the time he was through the door it was gone, not gradually but at once.

What is a mirror for? Not admiration. You look in one to find what needs attention: the smudge, the collar, the thing you cannot see without help. Scripture shows us what we really are, and its value lies in what you do in the ten seconds after you turn away. The man in the illustration has performed the ritual of self-examination and skipped the point of it, confusing looking with acting.

The face that shows us ours. The word does its sharpest work as a mirror when it shows us Christ. Peter had heard Jesus teach from his boat; then he saw the nets break, fell at Jesus’ knees and said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8). He had looked at Jesus, and seen himself. Scripture exposes us not chiefly by a list of faults but by setting the Holy One before us. And the mirror that exposes us is the one in which, beholding the glory of the Lord, we are slowly made like him (2 Corinthians 3:18). Jesus did not leave Peter on his knees: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men” (Luke 5:10). The look that exposes is meant to lead straight into following, which the forgetful man never does.

How do I stop forgetting? Respond before you leave the mirror. When a passage or a sermon shows you something, act while the image is fresh: confess the sin there and then, send the apology that day, write the one thing you will do on a card you will see tomorrow. Tell someone, because things spoken aloud are harder to forget. Reread the passage the next morning. Forgetting is not usually a failure of memory but a failure to act quickly; what we act on, we remember.

Does the mirror only show my faults? No, and this matters for tender consciences. The Scripture that shows you your sin shows you your Saviour, and who you are in him: forgiven, adopted, loved. Whoever sees only condemnation in the mirror is not reading the whole of it. Look until you see both: what needs washing, and the one who washes.

verseByVerse.quote: But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The person who keeps looking into God’s word, the law that sets free, and does what it says, will be blessed in the very doing of it.

Looks into. To stoop down and peer in, a stronger verb than in verse 23, used of Peter, John and Mary Magdalene bending to look into the empty tomb (Luke 24:12; John 20:5, 11): not a glance in passing but a posture. Peter uses it of angels longing to look into the salvation the prophets foretold (1 Peter 1:12). Angels stoop to look into this salvation; we are allowed to stoop and look, and to stay.

The perfect law. Complete, mature: God’s word, including the moral law as fulfilled and interpreted by Christ, the royal law of love (2:8).

The law of liberty. It sounds like a contradiction and is not. James does not mean law as a way of earning God’s favour; he has just said the implanted word saves. He means God’s revealed will as it now stands in Christ, which liberates because it is no longer a standard you must reach to be accepted. It is written on the heart by the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33) and obeyed from love, not compulsion: true freedom is the freedom to do what is right, released from slavery to sin (Romans 8:2). You keep it as a freed man, not as a slave earning his way out. And the law of liberty also judges (2:12).

And perseveres. To remain beside, to stay bent over it, the exact opposite of “goes away”. The difference between the two men is not the quality of the looking. One of them stayed.

A doer who acts. Literally “a doer of work”: for James, real obedience always leaves something done.

Blessed in his doing. As in verse 12. Not blessed for it, as though the doing purchased a reward, but in it: the blessing is inside the obedience (John 13:17; Psalm 1:1–3). The doing is itself the good thing, which the man walking away from the mirror never discovers.

If you abide in my word. Jesus joined staying and freedom first. “If you abide in my word,” he told those who had believed him, “you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free”; and “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:31–32, 36). The law’s freedom is not in the commandments by themselves but in the Son who kept them for us and stands behind every one as a friend, not an accuser. The man who stays bent over the word is staying with Christ, and that is where freedom lives.

Which law is this? Are Christians under the Ten Commandments? Christians are not under the law as a covenant of works, a way of earning acceptance or facing condemnation; Christ has fulfilled it and borne its curse for us (Galatians 3:13). But the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in love for God and neighbour, remains the rule of life for believers, showing us God’s will and our duty (Westminster Confession 19.6; 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.6). That is what James means: not the ceremonial laws of temple and sacrifice, which Christ fulfilled, but God’s holy will as Jesus taught it. Kept in love, it is not a cage but a road.

Does obedience always feel blessed? Not always at the time. Forgiving someone who hurt you, telling the truth when it costs, giving when money is tight: these can feel like loss. The blessing James means is deeper than a pleasant feeling: the quiet rightness of walking with God, a clear conscience, fruit that grows over time, God’s presence and help in the very act. Often it is recognised only looking back. But no one who has obeyed God has, in the end, regretted it.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person’s religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Religion God accepts is shown not by observances but by a bridled tongue, practical care for the helpless and a life kept clean from the world’s ways.

If anyone thinks he is religious. Thinks means supposes, seems to himself. Religious refers to religion’s outward exercise: observances, worship, visible practice. He attends, prays, fasts, and considers himself spiritual. James does not sneer at it. He asks what it is worth, and answers startlingly, first negatively (v. 26) and then positively (v. 27).

In the flow. These verses put “be doers of the word” (v. 22) to three tests, each opening a later part of the letter: the tongue (ch. 3), care for those with nothing to give (2:1–17), and friendship with the world (4:4).

Does not bridle his tongue. The bridle is the image of 3:2–3. Gossip, slander, harshness and lies contradict every religious claim. And of all the failures he could have chosen as the disqualifier, James chose speech, a sin most congregations tolerate entirely.

Worthless. Self-deception again (v. 22). Worthless means empty, futile, and it is said not of an unbeliever but of a churchgoer with a loose mouth.

Pure and undefiled. Terms of ritual purity, which James fills with practical love and moral holiness, as the prophets had done: “Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean,” Isaiah cried, and “plead the widow’s cause” (Isaiah 1:16–17). “Before God the Father” means what God, not people, counts as genuine. His is the only audience that matters.

Orphans and widows. The standard biblical shorthand for those with little legal protection and no income; a woman without husband or sons often had no one to go to court for her. God is their defender: “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5; Deuteronomy 10:18). To visit is to look after, to see to their needs; the word is related to the word for overseer. It does not mean sending money from a distance. It means turning up.

Unstained from the world. Two things usually pulled apart by people who prefer one: care for the defenceless, and personal holiness. James joins them with an “and” and gives no permission to choose. Unstained means spotless. The world here is human society organised in rebellion against God, with its values, desires and pressures (4:4; 1 John 2:15–17).

God has visited his people. The verb has a history. When Jesus stopped a funeral at the gate of Nain, had compassion on a widow burying her only son, and gave the young man back to his mother, the crowd cried, “God has visited his people!” (Luke 7:11–16). True religion visits widows because the God of true religion did, in the person of his Son, and did not send help from a distance. Our visiting is his visitation still going on through his people.

We were orphans. And the Father adopted us. The Son came down into the world’s filth, touched lepers and ate with sinners without being stained, then took our stains onto himself on the cross, so that we could be presented holy and blameless and above reproach (Colossians 1:22). Pure and undefiled religion is the family likeness of a Father who has visited us.

How does this apply today? In caring for orphans through adoption and fostering, for single mothers, for the lonely elderly and the widows in the church, in personal kindness and in the church’s organised care. And keeping oneself unstained means refusing the world’s values: its greed, its pride, its view of sex, its contempt for the weak. Who near you has no one to go to court for them, the widow, the foster child, the lonely old man, and when did you last turn up at their door?

What it does not mean. Not that caring for the needy is the whole of religion, or that worship and doctrine do not matter. James assumes faith in Christ (2:1), and says that those who believe that God is one “do well” (2:19). He is naming the test of genuine faith, as opposed to empty ritual. If you want to know whether the word has been implanted, do not look at the intensity of the hearing. Look at whether anyone with nothing to offer you has seen you lately.

Is caring for the needy the same as preaching the gospel? No. Nothing replaces telling people what Christ has done for sinners (Romans 10:14). But mercy is the fruit and adornment of the gospel, and a church that preaches grace and ignores the widow down the street contradicts its own message. Begin with the household of faith (Galatians 6:10), the widows and the struggling in your own church, and then go out to the neighbour. Word and deed belong together, as in Jesus’ ministry.

Does unstained from the world mean I should withdraw from society? No. Jesus prayed not that his people be taken out of the world but kept from the evil one (John 17:15), and visiting orphans and widows takes you right into the world’s mess. Being unstained means going into the hospital, the care home, the hard estate, without absorbing the greed, cynicism and lust the world takes for granted. As Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners and was never stained by their sin (Hebrews 7:26), the Christian goes in close and stays clean, by God’s grace.
