keyVerse.quote: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.
keyVerse.note: This is the thesis of the whole letter, and the rest of James applies it. It gathers up the chapter: the word that gave new birth (v. 18) and was planted in us (v. 21) is meant to be lived, and the trials, the tongue and the widow are where it is lived. Its sharpest warning is that the hearer who never does is not a hypocrite fooling others but a man fooling himself.

1.reflection:
James tells us to “count it all joy” in trials (v. 2), and the verb means to reckon, not to feel. How does that change the way you might respond to a trial you are in now? What would it look like to let steadfastness have its full effect instead of escaping, numbing or growing bitter?

The double-minded man asks God for wisdom while keeping his options open (vv. 6–8). Is there an area of your life where you have quietly decided God will not have the final word? What would it take to surrender it?

James traces sin from desire to death (vv. 14–15) and then sets against it the God who gives every good gift and brought us forth by his word (vv. 17–18). Why does it matter so much, in the moment of temptation, what we believe about God’s character?

The forgetful hearer looks intently into the mirror and walks away unchanged (vv. 23–24). What has God shown you in his word recently that you have not yet acted on? Who near you, like the widow or the orphan, has nothing to give you and needs you to turn up (v. 27)?

2.title: No Partiality: Faith That Sees Every Person
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 called us to be doers of the word (1:22–27). Chapter 2 tests that at two points: how the church treats the poor man at the door, and whether the faith we claim does anything at all.

The message. Faith in the Lord of glory cannot live alongside favouritism, and it cannot stay words. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, so ranking people by their clothes is sin against the royal law of love. And a faith that says the right things but never moves the hands is not a weaker kind of faith; it is dead. The faith that saves always works.

Why it was said. The readers were mostly poor and dragged into court by the rich (see the introduction), yet when a rich man walked into their meeting they still fawned on him. Like every church, they also had members who could recite the creed and supposed that was all faith required.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–13 forbid partiality: the scene at the door (vv. 1–4); three reasons it is senseless (vv. 5–7); the royal law of love, which one broken command breaks whole (vv. 8–11); and the judgment where mercy triumphs (vv. 12–13). Verses 14–26 ask what kind of faith saves: a blessing without bread (vv. 14–17), the demons’ faultless creed (vv. 18–19), Abraham, counted righteous long before he offered Isaac (vv. 20–24), and Rahab the Gentile prostitute (v. 25). Faith without works is a body without breath (v. 26). The poor visitor joins the two halves: a faith that shows him no love is dead faith.

Where it leads. To the Lord of glory (v. 1), who never judged by the face, but took the footstool and seated beggars beside him. He kept the whole law his people broke and bore its judgment, so that mercy triumphs without justice being set aside. And he is the Lamb God provided on the mountain where Abraham’s hand was stopped: Abraham’s faith was completed by his works, but our salvation was completed by God’s.

For us. James and Paul are not at odds: we are justified by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone (see the note on vv. 23–24). So look at the door: whom do you notice first, and whom never? And look at your hands: is there someone you have blessed with words and not yet helped?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Gold Ring and the Royal Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Favouritism contradicts faith in the Lord of glory, and the royal law of love condemns it. James paints two visitors, one seated in honour and one sent to the floor (vv. 1–4), then shows how senseless it is: God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, while the rich oppress the church and blaspheme Christ’s name (vv. 5–7). Love of neighbour leaves no room for ranking, and one broken command makes a transgressor of the whole law (vv. 8–11). So speak and act as those who will be judged by the law of liberty, where the merciful find that mercy triumphs over judgment (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology:
One Lawgiver

Partiality contradicts faith in the Lord of glory and breaks the royal law. Whoever fails at one point is guilty before the one who gave the whole law. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The congregation seated the man with the gold ring well and the poor man on the floor (see vv. 2–4).

Now: The sin includes ranking people inside a welcome (see the note on vv. 2–4).

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, cannot go together with favouritism.

My brothers, show no partiality. Partiality means letting the look of a person decide how you treat them; the Greek word is built on a Hebrew idiom, to receive or lift the face. Its home is the courtroom: the law forbade a judge to be partial to the poor or defer to the great (Leviticus 19:15), and grounded that in God himself, who is not partial and takes no bribe (Deuteronomy 10:17). James is about to describe a congregation behaving like a corrupt court.

As you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. The man accused of preaching works opens his great chapter on works with faith in Jesus, and favouritism contradicts that faith, as the rest of the verse shows.

The Lord of glory. The highest thing James says about his brother anywhere in the letter (on the wording, see the box below), for glory belongs to God alone: “I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other” (Isaiah 42:8). To give Jesus that glory is to call him God.

The placing is the argument. Beside that glory, the difference between a gold ring and a poor man’s rags is nothing. When the sun is up, nobody compares candles. A congregation that seats people by their clothes has forgotten who is in the room.

The man who grew up with him. James had sat at the same table as the Lord of glory for thirty years in Nazareth and seen a carpenter, and for a time did not believe in him at all (John 7:5). If anyone had learned that appearances mislead, it was James.

Brighter than any gold ring. The Lord of glory did not receive faces. He touched the leper, let a sinful woman weep on his feet, and called a despised little man down from a tree to host him. When he chose his people, he did not choose by our clothes; he clothed us in his own righteousness, so that the poorest beggar who trusts him stands in garments brighter than any gold ring. Glory belongs to him alone, and he spends it on the lowly.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all distinctions, such as honouring elders or respecting authorities (Romans 13:7). It forbids treating people differently because of wealth, status, race or appearance, especially in the church.

What does partiality look like in a church today? The same sin: the visitor with a profession and a nice car invited to lunch while the one with a carrier bag gets a handshake; the gifted and articulate noticed for leadership while the faithful and quiet are passed over; a platform for celebrities and large donors that their character has not earned; the sense that some races or cultures are more our sort. It can run the other way: despising the wealthy or the educated is also judging by the face. Ask plainly: am I treating this person according to what Christ has made him, or according to what he can do for me?

Is it wrong to have closer friends at church? No. Jesus himself had Peter, James and John, and John was the disciple whom Jesus loved. The sin James names is not having friends but ranking people’s worth. Enjoy your friends, and keep the circle open on one side, so that the newcomer, the awkward and the poor are welcomed in as brothers and sisters, not tolerated at the edge.

Uncertain wording. The Greek is compressed, literally “our Lord Jesus Christ of the glory”, and how the last words attach is not certain. It may mean “our glorious Lord Jesus Christ”, or, as the ESV takes it, “the Lord of glory” (compare 1 Corinthians 2:8). Some read “the Glory” as a title: Jesus is God’s glory come to dwell among his people, as the cloud of glory once filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34; John 1:14). Every reading gives Jesus the glory that belongs to God.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in, and if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” while you say to the poor man, “You stand over there,” or, “Sit down at my feet,” have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ranking people by their clothes turns a church into a corrupt court, with its members sitting as judges of other people’s worth.

A man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing. The first man is gold-fingered: perhaps wearing many rings, or the gold ring that in Roman society marked rank. His clothing is literally shining. He has dressed to be noticed and ranked.

Comes into your assembly. The word is synagogue, the only place in the New Testament where a Christian meeting is called that. It may mean a worship service, or perhaps a church court gathered to settle disputes between members (1 Corinthians 6:1–6), which would make the courtroom language even sharper.

A poor man in shabby clothing. Shabby means filthy, the same root as the filthiness of 1:21: not modest or plain, but dirty, because he has nothing else and nowhere to wash it.

You sit here in a good place. Every eye goes to the shining coat, and James gives the treatment in direct speech. To the first: here, in a place of honour. To the second, two options, both an insult: stand at the back, or sit on the floor, literally under my footstool, down where a servant or a dog would be.

A genuine welcome. Nobody is thrown out, and that is what makes the scene so recognisable: the sin is not exclusion but ranking, inside a genuine welcome. Nobody in that room would have said they were against the poor. They gave him a place; they just made sure he knew which one. Underneath lies a hunger of the heart: we honour the people whose approval we want, and we want it so badly because we have not yet rested in the approval of God, who has already welcomed us in Christ.

Have you not then made distinctions among yourselves. A church that sorts people has divided itself, and the double-mindedness of chapter 1 is coming out in the seating (see the box below).

And become judges with evil thoughts? Back to the courtroom of verse 1: literally judges whose reasonings are wicked. They have not merely been rude. They have tried both men on the evidence of their clothing and delivered verdicts on their worth, precisely what the law forbids a judge to do.

Christ took the footstool. He who has heaven as his throne and earth as his footstool (Isaiah 66:1) was born where animals ate and died stripped of his clothes while soldiers threw dice for them. He took the poor man’s place, so that we who stood in filthy rags before God could hear him say: take away his filthy garments, and clothe him with pure vestments (Zechariah 3:4). And then he says to the beggar he has dressed: “You sit here in a good place.” Sit with me on my throne (Revelation 3:21).

The oldest snobbery. We still turn towards the famous and give the well-dressed the benefit of every doubt. Adam Smith, the founder of modern economics, saw it. In The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) he called our disposition to admire, and almost to worship, the rich and the powerful, while neglecting the poor, the great and most universal cause of the corruption of our moral sentiments. We court those whose favour we think can make us someone, trying to borrow a worth we do not have. The gospel ends the borrowing. The Lord of glory has already seated us beside him, freely, and people who know where they are seated no longer need to be seen next to anyone else.

But what if a wealthy visitor could really help the church? That is exactly the thought James is exposing, dressed up as good stewardship. God has never needed a gold ring to provide for his work. Welcome the wealthy visitor as warmly as anyone else, and no more. If he is courted for his money, he learns that the church is like every other club, and the poor man learns it too.

What about someone who is dirty, smells, or is disruptive? Greet them, sit with them, offer a drink and something to eat. If someone is genuinely disruptive or unsafe, elders and stewards should deal with it calmly and kindly, because protecting the congregation, especially children, is also love. But the default is honour. The man in shabby clothes may be the one Christ sends to see how we treat him (Matthew 25:40).

In everyday life. Walk through your Sunday as a stranger with no money and no Christian vocabulary: where would you sit, and would anyone ask your name? Then be the one who does: sit next to the person nobody sits next to, learn their name, and find out one thing about their week.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “made distinctions” (diakrinō) usually means to distinguish or judge between, but in this form it can also mean to waver or doubt, as it does in 1:6. So James may mean “made distinctions among yourselves” or “wavered within yourselves”, divided between faith in Christ and the world’s way of ranking people. The ESV’s reading fits the courtroom language that follows, and the echo of 1:6 is probably intended as well.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man. Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, while the rich are the ones oppressing the church, so to shame the poor and fawn on the rich is both sinful and senseless. James gives three reasons, each sharper than the last.

Has not God chosen those who are poor in the world. The first argument is from what God has done. Chosen is the language of election; poor in the world means poor by worldly standards. Poverty qualifies no one, and not every poor person is saved, but this is how God has in fact worked: in the early church not many were wise or powerful or of noble birth (1 Corinthians 1:26). God has been choosing exactly the people this congregation is seating on the floor.

To be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom. Rich and poor have changed places: the man in the filthy coat may be the wealthiest person in the room, an heir of God’s reign, now and fully in the age to come (Matthew 5:3; 25:34), and “those who love him” is the phrase of 1:12 for true believers. The poor believer is a future king; the congregation is making a prince sit on the floor.

But you have dishonored the poor man. That is the charge, and the word is strong: to shame, to treat as worthless the very person God has honoured.

Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court? The second argument is brutally practical. Oppress means exploit, tyrannise, and these are not hypothetical rich men: chapter 5 will describe employers withholding the wages of the men who mowed their fields (5:1–6). To drag is to haul by force, as Paul and Silas were dragged into the marketplace before the rulers (Acts 16:19), perhaps over debts, perhaps because of their faith.

Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called? The third argument goes deepest. The honourable name, literally the beautiful name, is Christ’s, called over them as his own (see the question below). So the visitor being ushered to the good seat belongs to the class that exploits this congregation, takes it to court and insults its Lord.

The irrationality of flattery. James is not saying rich people are beyond salvation, nor telling the church to snub them; verse 1 forbids that too. He is showing how senseless the flattery is: they are fawning on people who despise them and mock their Lord, because of a ring.

Chosen in his Chosen One. God’s choice of the poor is not a social policy; it is the shape of the gospel, because his Chosen One came poor. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), and the Father said of him, “This is my Son, my Chosen One” (Luke 9:35). That is why the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3): it is the kingdom of a King who emptied his hands first. God’s choice runs downward: a slave nation, a shepherd boy, a peasant girl in Nazareth, fishermen in Galilee; and he chose us when we had nothing to offer him but our sin. A congregation that despises the poor man is despising the likeness of its own Lord.

Does God love the poor more than the rich? God chooses no one for their bank balance, any more than for their goodness: election is of grace alone (Romans 11:5–6). But he has a special care for the poor and the oppressed, and he often chooses the weak to shame the strong, so that no one may boast (1 Corinthians 1:27–29). The rich face a particular danger, because it is hard for them to feel their need (Matthew 19:23–26). The poor have often found it easier to come with empty hands, because their hands were already empty.

What does it mean that Christ’s name was called over me? James says literally that the name “was called over you”, and it means you belong to him. In the Old Testament, to have God’s name called over a people, a city or the temple meant that God owned it and would defend it (Deuteronomy 28:10; Jeremiah 14:9). In the church this is marked in baptism (Acts 2:38), into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19): you carry his name. So treat others, and let yourself be treated, as people whose worth is set by the one whose name they wear.

In everyday life. Think of someone in your church who is poor in the world. God sees them as rich in faith and an heir of the kingdom, so go and learn from them: ask them how God has kept them.

verseByVerse.quote: If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Loving your neighbour as yourself, the King’s own law, leaves no room for ranking people, so favouritism is not a social lapse but sin. The very law the readers might plead in their defence is the one that convicts them.

If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture. James anticipates the defence: we were being hospitable; we were loving our neighbour. “Really” means “if in fact”. Royal probably means the King’s law, belonging to the kingdom just mentioned (v. 5; see the box below).

You shall love your neighbor as yourself. He grants the principle, quoting Leviticus 19:18, which sums up the commandments about how we treat other people (Romans 13:8–10). And look where James found it: three verses after Leviticus 19:15, the very prohibition of partiality in judgment. Readers who knew their Scriptures would hear both halves of one paragraph.

But if you show partiality, you are committing sin. Then the trap closes: whichever man you seated well, you did not treat the other as yourself. That is not a social failure but sin.

And are convicted by the law as transgressors. Back to the courtroom a third time, and now the seating committee is in the dock. They set themselves up as judges (v. 4); now the law they claim to keep tries them. Convicted means proved guilty, and a transgressor is one who has stepped over a line that was drawn and marked.

The King’s law and the King’s love. Jesus set Leviticus 19:18 beside the command to love God as the two on which all the Law and the Prophets depend (Matthew 22:37–40), and at the Last Supper he gave it a new measure: “just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another” (John 13:34). The standard is no longer only “as yourself”, but as he loved, by washing feet and laying down his life. Like the Samaritan in his own parable, he crossed the road to us when we lay half dead, poured in oil and wine, carried us on his own beast and paid for our care. The seating committee is being judged by the law of a King who knelt.

Does love your neighbour as yourself mean I must learn to love myself first? No. The command assumes that we already love ourselves: we naturally feed, protect and want good things for ourselves (Ephesians 5:29). It does not command self-esteem; it turns that care outward. Many who feel they hate themselves are in fact very focused on themselves; the cure is the love of God, which frees us to forget ourselves and attend to others.

Who counts as my neighbour? Jesus answered with the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37): whoever God puts in your path who needs your help, including the person of another race, class or religion, and the one you would naturally avoid. The lawyer wanted to limit the list; Jesus asked instead who proved to be a neighbour. In James’s scene the neighbour is the man in the filthy coat.

What does loving my neighbour as myself look like? The command hands you its own measuring stick: think how you want to be treated, and do that (Matthew 7:12). Go first to the newcomer, the one on the edge, the one in the shabby coat. Give time and attention, not only money. Speak about people as you would want to be spoken about when you are not in the room. Meet the practical need you can meet: the meal, the lift, the form filled in (2:15–16). And keep going when it costs, since you do not stop caring for yourself when you are inconvenient to yourself. None of this is the price of God’s favour. We were the man in the filthy coat, and Christ did not wait for us to become presentable. People who have been seated that kindly learn to seat others.

Uncertain wording. Why the law is called “royal” is not certain. It may be the supreme law, ruling all the others, as Jesus made love the summary of the Law; or the law given by the King himself; or the law of the kingdom whose heirs the poor believers are (v. 5). The ideas overlap, and the likely sense holds them together: the King’s own law for his kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it. For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is one because the Lawgiver is one, so breaking any command, partiality included, makes you a lawbreaker before him.

For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point. That sounds disproportionate; everything depends on seeing why it is not. Fails means stumbles, even once.

Has become guilty of all of it. Guilty means liable, answerable. The law is like a single sheet of glass: a pane with one hole in it is a broken window, not a mostly intact one.

For he who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not murder. The reasoning is about the lawgiver rather than the law. One voice stands behind every command (Exodus 20:13–14; Deuteronomy 5:17–18), so the law is not a list from which you might keep most and fail a few, but the expression of one person’s will. Break any of it and you have set yourself against the one who spoke.

If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law. Adultery and murder were the sins the congregation would condemn most readily. James sets them beside seating the poor man on the floor: same court, same lawgiver, same verdict.

The grading of sins. The argument takes away our private ranking of sins by how disreputable they look, in which our own (the impatience, the snobbery, the gossip, the little dishonesties) sit comfortably near the bottom. Partiality feels like a lapse of etiquette; James has just put it in a sentence with murder. That is humbling, and it is also freeing: the person whose sins are louder than yours is standing at the same cross as you, and the same blood covers you both.

The same voice has spoken again. The Lawgiver who said “Do not commit adultery” and “Do not murder” came under his own law, kept every point of it, and was counted guilty of all of it in the place of his people. We never keep it whole, not even on our best days; the window we smashed was paid for with his blood, and now his obedience, whole and unbroken, is counted as ours. The glass is not patched; it is replaced with his. And the voice that thundered from Sinai said from the cross, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), and, “It is finished” (John 19:30).

What it does not mean. Not that all sins are equally serious in every respect: Scripture recognises degrees of sin and punishment (John 19:11; Luke 12:47–48). The point is narrower and sharper: every sin puts you in the same relation to the same God, and no amount of law-keeping makes up for the part broken.

Then what hope does anyone have? None in the law, and that is what the law is meant to teach: if one failure makes us guilty of all, a lifetime of mostly keeping the rules cannot save anyone. Our only hope is the substitute described above: born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5), he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). James is not preaching despair. He is closing every other door so that we go through the only open one.

If I am already guilty of all, does it matter if I sin a little more? It matters enormously. Every sin offends the God who loves you, damages you and others, and grieves the Spirit (Ephesians 4:30); the point is that every sin matters more than we think. A forgiven believer does not reason: since I am covered, I may as well. He reasons: since he paid so much, how can I go on in what he died for (Romans 6:1–2)?

verseByVerse.quote: So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers will still face God’s judgment, so let mercy shape everything you say and do: a merciless life will meet judgment without mercy, but mercy triumphs over judgment.

So speak and so act. Both verbs mean keep on doing so, and speaking comes first in a letter this concerned with speech; the seating in verse 3 was done with words.

As those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. The phrase is from 1:25: God’s will as it stands in Christ, written on the heart and kept by people already accepted. But it does not remove judgment: the freed man is still to be judged, and should live accordingly.

For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. This restates the Lord’s own teaching: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy” (Matthew 5:7), and the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35). Read it the right way round. A merciless person is not disqualified for failing to earn mercy; he is exposed. Mercy received produces mercy given, so a life with none flowing out shows that none has come in.

Mercy triumphs over judgment. To triumph is to exult over a defeated opponent. For those who have received mercy in Christ and show it, the judgment holds no terror. Judgment is real, mercy is stronger, and the congregation seating men by their clothing is being asked which of the two it has been imitating.

Where mercy and judgment met. How can mercy triumph without justice being thrown away? Only at the cross. There God did not set aside his judgment against sin; he poured it out in full on his Son, our substitute, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Mercy did not win by ignoring judgment, but by bearing it. And on the last day those who stand before the judgment seat will meet the Lamb who was slain for them, not a stranger weighing their record.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn God’s mercy by showing mercy. We show mercy because we have received it: “be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32).

Will Christians really be judged? Yes, but not for condemnation. There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Every believer will stand before the judgment seat of Christ, where our lives are opened and what was done in his name is acknowledged and rewarded (2 Corinthians 5:10; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). It is a Father’s assessment of his children, not a court deciding their fate: it should make us serious, never afraid that Christ will cast us out.

I find it very hard to forgive someone who hurt me. Does that mean I have not received mercy? Not necessarily. Forgiving deep wounds is often a long process, and the struggle itself shows that you want to obey; the merciless person James describes refuses and feels justified. Bring your hurt to God honestly, as the psalmists did, ask him for grace, and remember how much you have been forgiven. Forgiving means giving up your right to revenge and leaving judgment to God (Romans 12:19). It does not mean pretending it did not happen, or trusting the person again immediately.

Does showing mercy mean there should be no consequences? No. Mercy does not excuse evil. If someone is abusing you, seek safety at once; forgiving him does not mean staying in danger, keeping silent, or protecting him from the law. The authorities exist to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and churches must report abuse and protect the vulnerable. Mercy refuses personal revenge and longs for the offender’s repentance; justice still holds him accountable. A church that covers up abuse in the name of mercy is not showing mercy to anyone, least of all the victim.

In everyday life. James says “so speak”, so listen to yourself this week. When you talk about the colleague who failed you, or the brother whose sin embarrassed the church, do you sound like someone who has been forgiven much? Let that mercy reach your tongue first.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A faith that only talks cannot save; the faith that saves always works. Kind words to a hungry brother, with no food given, show what such faith is worth: it is dead (vv. 14–17). Faith cannot be shown except by what it does, and the demons’ faultless creed proves that right belief alone is not saving faith (vv. 18–19). Then Scripture settles it. Abraham, counted righteous when he believed, had that faith proved and completed when he offered Isaac (vv. 20–24), and Rahab the Gentile prostitute showed hers when she hid the spies (v. 25). As the body without the spirit is dead, so is faith without works (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith That Works

James asks whether a faith that is only said can save (see v. 14). Abraham was counted righteous by faith, and his obedience showed that faith was alive (see vv. 21–24). Works do not earn justification (see the note on vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The demons believe that God is one, and they shudder (see vv. 18–19).

Now: Warm words to a hungry brother with nothing given are the picture of dead faith (see vv. 15–17).

verseByVerse.quote: What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A faith that is only claimed, with no works to show for it, cannot save anyone. James is not asking whether faith saves, but whether this kind of faith does.

What good is it, my brothers. What profit, what use: the theme of the whole passage is useful faith against useless faith.

If someone says he has faith but does not have works? The first key word is says: a man who claims faith, and the question is whether the claim is true. Works here are the deeds of love and obedience that living faith produces, like clothing and feeding a poor brother (vv. 15–16). They are not works of the law, moral or ceremonial, offered to God as grounds for acceptance; those, Paul says, can never justify anyone (Romans 3:20; 4:4–5).

Can that faith save him? The second key word is “that”. The Greek has “the faith” (hē pistis): can the faith just described, that kind of faith, save him? The form of the question expects the answer no. A faith that consists only of words cannot save.

Back to back. Paul and James stand back to back, defending the same gospel on two sides (see the box at the end of this note). James contrasts not faith with works, but living faith with dead faith.

What faith holds. Both apostles assume that faith saves not by being impressive but by what it takes hold of: it is an empty hand, and Christ is the one it grasps. That is why the faith of verse 14 cannot save: it has words about Christ but has never closed on him. And no one can take hold of the Lord who went about doing good (Acts 10:38) and stay idle, any more than a branch joined to the vine can stay bare (John 15:5). The works James looks for are not a second hope beside Christ, but proof that he has been grasped.

What exactly is saving faith, then? Reformed teachers have long described it in three parts: knowledge of who Christ is and what he has done; agreement that it is true; and trust, resting on Christ personally for forgiveness and life. The faith James attacks has the first two at most and never comes to the third. True faith is a drowning man taking hold of the rope, and a man who has done that does not stay in the water.

What about the thief on the cross? He had no time for good works. He was saved by faith alone, and his faith was alive: in his last hours it rebuked the other criminal, confessed his own guilt, defended Jesus’ innocence and called on him as King (Luke 23:40–43). Works in James’s sense are not a quota to be filled before you qualify; they are the signs of life that appear wherever faith is real, however short the time. A newborn baby has achieved nothing, but it breathes and cries. So did the thief.

Where Christians differ: does James contradict Paul? Paul says we are justified by faith, not works (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16); James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (v. 24). Some have thought they contradict; Luther once called James an epistle of straw for this reason, though he kept it in his Bible and dropped the phrase from later editions of his preface. Roman Catholic teaching uses James to argue that justification includes good works. This commentary’s view: they do not contradict. They answer different errors and use key words in different senses. Paul opposes legalism: those who think they can earn God’s acceptance by works of the law. James opposes empty profession: those who think a faith with no fruit can save. For Paul, justify means God’s declaration that a sinner is righteous, received through faith alone; for James here, it means to show or prove righteous, as Abraham’s faith was vindicated by his deeds. For Paul, works means works of the law done to earn merit; for James, works of love that flow from faith. For Paul, faith means genuine trust in Christ; for James in verse 14, a mere claim to believe. Both agree that the faith which justifies always produces works (Galatians 5:6; Ephesians 2:8–10).
verseByVerse.note: Paul says we are justified by faith, not works; James says a faith that produces no works is not saving faith. They answer different errors.

verseByVerse.quote: If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A faith that blesses a hungry brother with words and sends him away empty is worth no more than that blessing: it is dead.

If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food. Not a stranger but someone in the congregation, and James explicitly includes women. Poorly clothed means naked, inadequately dressed; lacking in daily food means without food for today. This is not want of comfort.

And one of you says to them, Go in peace, be warmed and filled. The words are entirely correct. Go in peace is the ordinary Jewish farewell blessing, and the two verbs may be a wish used in prayer: may you be warmed, may you be filled. This man is quite possibly praying.

Without giving them the things needed for the body. He has said everything and done nothing, and the kind words make it grotesque; silence would have been less offensive.

What good is that? The question of verse 14 again, and now with a cold answer: the man is exactly as hungry as before, and has been sent away feeling blessed.

A coat and a meal. James could have picked adultery or theft to expose a hollow faith. He picks a coat and a meal, because the failure he describes is not scandalous: it is a religion that is fluent, warm, and costs nothing. John says the same: “let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:18).

So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead. By itself means alone. Not weak, not immature, but dead, which is a word about what a thing is, not how much of it there is. A corpse is not a person with reduced vitality.

A rescue, not a well-wishing. When we were naked and starving, God did not send us away with a blessing. He came: the Word became flesh, fed the hungry with his own hands, and gave his body as bread for the life of the world. His love was never words: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10), the sacrifice that bore God’s just anger against our sin and turned it away from us. The gospel is a rescue, and every coat given in his name is a small picture of it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith becomes alive by adding works, as if works gave life to faith. Works show that faith is alive. A living tree bears fruit; the fruit does not make it alive.

But if my works are weak and inconsistent, is my faith dead? James is describing a faith with no works at all, and he himself says we all stumble in many ways (3:2). Living faith may be small and imperfect, but it is real: it trusts Christ, it struggles against sin, and it shows itself, however feebly, in love.

Do I have to give to everyone who asks? James’s example is a brother or sister in real need, in front of you, and you able to help. Start there: the church family comes first (Galatians 6:10), and genuine need you can meet should be met. Beyond that, love uses wisdom. Money can feed an addiction, where a meal or a bag of shopping would not; and a man able to work but unwilling should not be fed for nothing (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Wisdom shapes how we help. It is never an excuse for not helping at all.

In everyday life. Is there someone you have wished well but not helped? Next time you say “I will pray for you”, consider whether you could also say: “And what can I bring round on Thursday?”

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith cannot be seen except in what it does, and right belief on its own is not saving faith, for the demons have it.

But someone will say, You have faith and I have works. James brings in an objector (on where his words end, see the box below). The likeliest sense is: “These are two gifts. You have faith, and I have works. Different people, different strengths, and both are fine.” James refuses to separate faith and works.

Show me your faith apart from your works. A challenge that cannot be met: faith is invisible, and there is no way to display it except through what it does.

And I will show you my faith by my works. Works are the visible evidence of invisible faith; you will recognise them by their fruits (Matthew 7:16–20).

You believe that God is one; you do well. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), recited by every devout Jew morning and evening. James picks the soundest statement of belief there is and grants it fully; he is not belittling right belief.

Even the demons believe, and shudder! The demons’ theology is faultless; in Mark’s Gospel they name Jesus correctly while the crowds are still asking who he is: “I know who you are, the Holy One of God” (Mark 1:24; 5:7). So right belief (orthodoxy) cannot be what distinguishes a Christian, because the demons have it and are not saved.

Orthodox and terrified. They shudder, the hair standing on end: the creed is right and the feelings are real, and it changes nothing, because they do not trust, love or obey. That should search anyone whose Christianity consists of correct beliefs and real feelings in a service, and nothing more.

The creed goes on to love. The demons hold the first line of the Shema and stop. But the Shema does not stop at “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.” It goes straight on: “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). Saving faith believes the creed all the way into love, and the New Testament shows where that love is fixed: Paul restates the Shema with Christ inside it, one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6). The demons know who Jesus is; only faith loves him. And the Holy One of God whom the demons named in terror is the friend of sinners.

How do I know my faith is more than the demons’ faith? The demons know Jesus is the Son of God and want him to go away (Mark 5:7); do you want him near? They tremble at God and hate him; do you, even weakly, love him and want to please him? They believe, and keep on rebelling; do you fight your sin, and grieve when you fail? If your heart comes to Christ, rests on him and wants to follow him, however feebly, that is not demonic belief but the work of the Spirit.

Should I look at my works to find assurance? Look first and chiefly to Christ, his promises and his finished work: that is the foundation of assurance. Then the change in your life confirms that your faith is real, and the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16). The Westminster Confession (18.2) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (18.2) teach the same. Look only at your works and you will become proud or despair; look to Christ, and you can look honestly at your life without fear, because your hope does not rest there.

Uncertain wording. Where the objector’s words end in verse 18 is uncertain, since ancient manuscripts carried no quotation marks, and the pronouns are puzzling: “you have faith” seems an odd thing to say to James. Some end the objection after “I have works”, as the ESV does; others extend it further, or take “you” and “I” loosely, as “one person has faith, another has works”. James’s reply is clear whatever the punctuation: faith and works cannot be parcelled out to different people, because faith can only be shown by its works.
verseByVerse.note: The confession “God is one” is the Shema, the daily creed of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A faith that does nothing is useless, and James rebukes the hollow believer sharply in order to fill him, not to dismiss him.

Do you want to be shown, you foolish person. “Want” means “are you willing”, and “foolish” means empty, hollow: it is aimed at a religion that is only a claim, with nothing inside it. It is a rebuke, not an insult; James means to fill what is empty, not to write the man off.

That faith apart from works is useless? Useless (argē) is a slight change from dead in verse 17. It means idle, out of employment: the term for land lying fallow or a labourer standing in the marketplace with nothing to do (Matthew 20:3). And there is a deliberate play in it: faith without works (ergōn) does not work (a-ergē).

O foolish ones. The rebuke has a precedent that shows its purpose. On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus said, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!” and then, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:25–27). The sharp word opened the book, and the book opened onto him. James follows the same order: he rebukes, then turns to Scripture, beginning with Abraham. And God does not leave empty people empty. He fills the hungry with good things (Luke 1:53), and the Spirit he has poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5) is the one who turns idle faith into working love.

Jesus said whoever says You fool will be liable to judgment. Is James breaking that rule? No. Jesus was forbidding contemptuous insult flung in anger (Matthew 5:22). James is giving a pastoral diagnosis, the way Jesus himself called the Pharisees blind fools (Matthew 23:17) and the Emmaus disciples foolish. The angry insult wants to wound and dismiss; the loving rebuke wants to wake someone up and bring him back. A friend who shouts as you step towards a cliff edge is not being cruel.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read dead here (as in vv. 17, 26), but useless is better supported; the KJV follows the later reading, faith without works is dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s offering of Isaac did not make him righteous; it proved that the faith by which he had long been counted righteous was real, and brought that faith to its full end.

Was not Abraham our father justified by works. Abraham is father of the Jewish people and of all who believe (Romans 4:11–12), and James chooses the same man Paul uses to prove justification by faith apart from works (Romans 4:1–5), and appears to say the opposite. But justified here means shown to be righteous, vindicated, proved genuine, in the ordinary sense Jesus used when he said “wisdom is justified by her deeds” (Matthew 11:19), and that we use when we say events justified someone’s confidence.

When he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? The order of events settles it, as James himself shows by quoting Genesis 15:6 (v. 23). Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, when he believed the promise about the stars. He offered Isaac in Genesis 22, many years later, probably decades. So the offering cannot be what made him righteous before God; it demonstrated and vindicated a faith already counted for righteousness. God said afterward that now he knew Abraham feared him (Genesis 22:12).

You see that faith was active along with his works. Verse 22 explains justified by works exactly. Faith was working together with his works: collaborators, not rivals, faith the source and works the expression.

And faith was completed by his works. Completed means brought to its intended end: not supplemented but fulfilled, as a seed is fulfilled in a tree.

The faith that raised the knife. Moriah tested Abraham’s faith to destruction, for the son on the altar was the very promise he had believed God for. Only a man who trusted God to keep his word could raise that knife. Hebrews tells us what he was thinking: “He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead” (Hebrews 11:17–19).

The Lamb God provided. On the mountain Isaac asked the question the whole Old Testament kept asking: the fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb? (Genesis 22:7). Abraham answered that God would provide. The answer came by the Jordan, centuries later, when John the Baptist pointed to Jesus and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). The ram died for one boy; the Lamb God provided died for all his people, and no voice from heaven stopped what was done to him. Abraham’s faith was completed by his works. Our salvation was completed by God’s.

Does the story of Isaac mean God approves of child sacrifice? No. God stopped Abraham’s hand and provided the ram, and his law later condemned child sacrifice as an abomination (Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 7:31). The command was a unique test, never to be repeated, designed to point forward. In the land of Moriah, where Solomon later built the temple (2 Chronicles 3:1), not far from where Jesus would die, God would one day not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32). What God stopped Abraham from doing, he did himself, for us.

Will God test me the way he tested Abraham? Not with that command; God will never ask you to do what his word forbids. But he does test whether we love him more than his gifts, often in the thing we most treasure: a child, a career, a hope. He may ask you to hold it with an open hand, and to obey him when obedience seems to put it at risk. The lesson of Moriah is that God can be trusted with our Isaacs: the LORD will provide (Genesis 22:14). And if you have lost a child, hear this gently: your loss is not a test you failed or a price God demanded. The Father who did not spare his own Son knows that grief from the inside, and he is near to you in it.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”—and he was called a friend of God. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God counted Abraham righteous when he believed, and his obedience years later showed that verdict to be true; so a person is shown to be righteous by works, and not by a faith that stays alone.

And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. James quotes Genesis 15:6, the very verse Paul builds Romans 4 on (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6). Counted means credited, imputed: an accounting word, for putting to someone’s account what was not his, as a gift is paid into an empty bank account. Abraham had no righteous record to offer; God counted righteousness to him apart from works (Romans 4:6). And fulfilled is the key, the word for a prophecy coming true, filled up to its full meaning. God had declared Abraham righteous; on Moriah that declaration was shown to be true.

And he was called a friend of God. The title comes from 2 Chronicles 20:7 and Isaiah 41:8, and it is still how Abraham is known across the Middle East today: in Arabic, simply the Friend. Look at what James thinks the offering produced: not merit, but intimacy. The God of glory calls such people his friends, and their friendship shows in obedience: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14).

You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. The most debated phrase in James: the only place in the New Testament where “faith alone” appears, and here it is denied. But read what James denies. Justified, as in verse 21, means shown to be righteous. Not by faith alone means not by the faith of verses 14–19, a faith on its own, a mere profession. A person is shown to be righteous by works that prove their faith real.

The counterfeit. James is not attacking justification by faith alone, which the Reformation recovered, but the counterfeit that always attaches itself to it: a belief that costs nothing and changes nothing. James guards the real thing by exposing the fake.

Counted for his sake and for ours. Paul draws out of the same verse what James assumes: the words “it was counted to him” were written not for Abraham’s sake alone, but for ours also, who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:23–25). The righteousness credited to a believing sinner is not his faith treated as a good work. It is Christ’s: for our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is the root. Abraham on Moriah is the fruit, and James will not let us have one without the other.

If I stop doing good works, will I lose my justification? No. God’s verdict of justification is given once for all, rests entirely on Christ’s righteousness, and cannot be reversed: “those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30). Those truly justified will persevere, because God keeps them (Philippians 1:6): a believer may fall into serious sin and be disciplined by his Father, but he will not finally fall away. If someone abandons Christ completely and permanently, it shows his faith was never the living kind (1 John 2:19). The answer to coldness is not fear of losing justification but returning to the Saviour who justified you.

Can I really be God’s friend? Yes. Abraham was a sinner who lied about his wife twice, and God called him friend. Jesus says to his disciples: “No longer do I call you servants … but I have called you friends” (John 15:15). Friendship with God is not reserved for spiritual giants but given to everyone justified by faith: you may speak to him freely, trust his heart and enjoy his company, and it shows itself, as Abraham’s did, in trusting obedience.

Is it not a legal fiction for God to count a sinner righteous? It would be a fiction only if nothing real stood behind the verdict. But the righteousness counted to the believer is Christ’s, really lived in a perfect life and really paid for in a real death (see above). Faith joins us to him, as a bride to her husband, and what is his becomes ours: his name, his record, his standing with the Father. And the God who declares a sinner righteous never leaves him as he found him; the Spirit who gives faith begins at once to make him new, which is exactly what James insists on.

Where Christians differ: does this verse deny justification by faith alone? Roman Catholic teaching cites this verse against the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone, to show that justification is a process of being made righteous, to which faith and works both contribute. Catholic teaching also insists that justification begins with God’s grace and not with human merit, and many Catholics sincerely love Christ; the disagreement is over what justification is. This commentary’s view: James is not denying that we are declared righteous by faith alone in Paul’s sense; he quotes Genesis 15:6 himself. Nor is he describing how a sinner is first accepted by God: he says that Abraham was counted righteous when he believed (v. 23), and then shows that faith proved true years later. He is denying that a faith which remains alone, without works, is saving faith. The Reformers said it well: we are justified by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone. James and Paul agree: God declares sinners righteous by grace through faith in Christ, on the basis of his righteousness imputed to them; and the faith that receives this always works by love.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, many years before he offered Isaac in Genesis 22; the offering showed the faith was real.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rahab, a Gentile prostitute, proved her faith real by risking her life for God’s people, and faith without such works is as dead as a body without breath.

And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works. The second example is as unlike the first as possible. Abraham is a man, the father of the nation, the friend of God. Rahab is a woman, a Gentile, a Canaanite and a prostitute, and James does not soften the noun. Between them they cover everybody. And a congregation that seats men by their clothes is shown two people God justified, one of whom it would not have let through the door: a woman Matthew lists among King David’s ancestors.

When she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? She received them as guests; she hid the two spies under flax on her roof; and she sent them out (a strong word, thrust out) by a different route, so that they escaped (Joshua 2:1–21). It was treason, punishable by death, done on the strength of what she had heard about Israel’s God: “the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). Hebrews 11:31 credits the same act to faith, so James and Hebrews are looking at one event from two sides.

For as the body apart from the spirit is dead. Spirit also means breath. A body without breath is a corpse.

So also faith apart from works is dead. The conclusion, repeating verse 17. Faith is the body, and works are the breath that shows a body is alive. A faith with no works is a corpse: the shape is all there, the features are recognisable, and nothing is moving.

The prostitutes go in first. Rahab’s place in the story is not an embarrassment but the gospel. Matthew names her in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). And Jesus told the chief priests that “the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you”, because when John came they believed him and you did not (Matthew 21:31–32). The Lord who came from her line came for her kind, and his kingdom is still entered the way she entered Israel.

On the third day he breathed again. When Jericho fell, a woman whose house was built into the wall, with a scarlet cord in its window, walked out alive with her family, with nothing to plead but faith (Joshua 6:22–25). That is how everyone comes out of the ruin. The Lord breathed his last on a cross for prostitutes and patriarchs alike, and on the third day he breathed again; on the evening of his rising he breathed on his disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Living faith breathes because the risen Christ has breathed into it, and what he has made alive he will never let die.

But Rahab lied. She lied to the king’s men (Joshua 2:4–5). James commends her faith, shown in receiving the spies and sending them out safely (Hebrews 11:31), not the lie as such. Christians differ on whether deceiving those bent on murder is a sin; either way, it was her faith that God honoured, and ordinary lying is still sin.

My past is like Rahab’s. Can my faith be real? Yes, and this verse was written partly for you. God did not wait for Rahab to clean up her reputation. She believed with what little she knew, acted on it, and was brought into the family line of the Messiah. Your past does not limit his grace; it magnifies it. The question is not where you have been but whom you are trusting now, and whether that trust is starting to move your hands and feet.

What does a living faith look like in an ordinary week? Usually it is quiet: the young mother who prays while she changes nappies and is patient with a toddler for Christ’s sake, the businessman who refuses the dishonest deal, the teenager who sits with the lonely kid at lunch, the old man who visits the hospital every Thursday, the couple who open their home to the church’s newcomers. Rahab’s work was one dangerous night, but most works of faith are small, repeated and unseen. They are the breathing of a living faith, and breathing is rarely dramatic. It is only noticed when it stops.
