Mercy triumphs over judgment.<sup>14</sup>What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?<sup>15</sup>If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food,<sup>16</sup>and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?<sup>17</sup>So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.<sup>18</sup>But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works.<sup>19</sup>You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!<sup>20</sup>Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?<sup>21</sup>Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar?<sup>22</sup>You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works;<sup>23</sup>and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”—and he was called a friend of God.<sup>24</sup>You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.<sup>25</sup>And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way?<sup>26</sup>For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.

keyVerse.quote: So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.
keyVerse.note: This verdict joins the two halves of the chapter. The church that blesses a hungry brother and sends him away empty, like the church that seats the poor man on the floor, has a faith that talks and does not move. James does not call such faith weak but dead: living faith is known by its breath, and its breath is love.

2.reflection:
James pictures a congregation that welcomes the poor man but makes sure he knows his place (vv. 2–4). Where might our church, or you personally, rank people without ever excluding them? Whose approval are we hoping to win when we do?

God has chosen the poor in the world to be rich in faith (v. 5). Who in your church is poor in the world but rich in faith, and what could you learn from them?

James puts partiality in the same sentence as adultery and murder (vv. 9–11). Which sins do you quietly treat as minor? How does the cross change the way you see both your own sins and other people’s?

James says that faith without works is dead (vv. 17, 26), yet Abraham was counted righteous before he did anything (v. 23). How would you explain to a friend how James and Paul fit together? Is there someone you have wished well but not helped (vv. 15–16)?

3.title: The Tongue and True Wisdom
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 tested faith by what it does; chapter 3 takes the test to the place it is hardest to pass, the mouth, and then to the wisdom behind it. It develops two themes of the letter’s overture: the bridled tongue (1:19, 26) and the wisdom God gives to those who ask (1:5).

The message. Your words show what you are, and you cannot put them right by effort. The tongue is small but steers a whole life; it is a fire lit from hell, and no human being can tame it. Worse, the same mouth blesses God and curses the people who bear his likeness. A spring that gives both fresh and salt water has something wrong at its source. So the answer is not a technique but a new source: the wisdom that comes down from above, known not by cleverness but by a pure, peaceable, gentle and merciful life.

Why it was said. Too many in these congregations wanted to teach (v. 1), and the scattered, hard-pressed churches (see the introduction) were being harmed less by persecutors outside than by their own talk inside: envy, rivalry and quarrels, which chapter 4 traces to their root (4:1).

How the chapter makes its case. A warning to would-be teachers (vv. 1–2) widens to everyone: we all stumble, most of all in speech. Three pictures show the tongue’s power, the bit, the rudder and the spark (vv. 3–5); three more show its evil: a fire lit from hell (v. 6), an untameable poison (vv. 7–8), and a mouth that blesses and curses (vv. 9–10). Three questions from nature, the spring, the tree and the salt pond, move the problem from the mouth to its source (vv. 11–12). Then James sets two wisdoms side by side. The claim to be wise is tested by meekness (v. 13); envy and ambition are a wisdom from below, and they leave disorder behind (vv. 14–16); the wisdom from above is pure, then peaceable, and those who make peace sow a harvest of righteousness (vv. 17–18). The chapter that begins with a fire set by hell ends with a harvest sown from heaven.

Where it leads. To the one man who never stumbled in what he said (v. 2). When he was reviled, he did not revile in return, and from the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). No human being can tame the tongue, but the Son of God became a human being and did. He is the wisdom from above in person, “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and the great Peacemaker who made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). He gives what James says we cannot produce: a new heart, a new spring, and tongues lit from heaven instead of hell.

For us. Listen to yourself for a day, and treat what comes out as evidence about your heart. Then do not merely resolve to speak better: ask God for the wisdom he has promised (1:5), and go and make peace with someone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your words reveal and steer your whole life, and no human effort can master them, because the trouble lies at the source. A warning to would-be teachers opens onto everyone: we all stumble, above all in speech (vv. 1–2). The tongue is small but decisive, like a bit or a rudder (vv. 3–4), and destructive, like a spark in a forest, lit from hell (vv. 5–6). Man has tamed every creature but cannot tame it (vv. 7–8), and the same mouth blesses God and curses people made in his likeness (vv. 9–10). Spring, tree and salt pond show that speech reveals its source (vv. 11–12), which prepares for the wisdom from above.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Tongue Cannot Be Tamed

The tongue is small and decisive (see vv. 3–4), and no human can tame it (see vv. 7–8). The problem is the spring, not the water (see the note on vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Too many in the congregation wanted to teach.

Now: We cannot bless God and curse people made in his likeness from the same mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teaching God’s word is a weighty calling, not a platform, so few should rush into it. Those who teach will answer to God more strictly, because their words shape other people’s souls.

Not many of you. A startling opening: too many in that congregation wanted the job. Teachers held a recognised and respected role (Acts 13:1). Among Jews the rabbi was among the most honoured figures in the community, and in scattered congregations with no settled structure the man who could hold a room had an obvious opportunity.

We who teach. James puts himself inside the warning. Greater strictness is literally a greater judgment: to whom much is given, much is required (Luke 12:48). A teacher handles other people’s souls with his words, and error from the front does damage that error in private conversation does not. Teachers answer both for what they teach and for how they live (Matthew 12:36–37), because their hearers copy both.

The wanting. James does not discourage the gift, which the New Testament commands and prizes, but the wanting: the drift toward a visible role for reasons that have more to do with standing than with service.

You have one teacher. James’s warning echoes his brother’s: do not be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers; you have one instructor, the Christ (Matthew 23:8–10). Every teacher in the church is a pupil first, under the one Teacher, who will never be judged, because he is the Judge, and whose words were never once careless. “No one ever spoke like this man!” (John 7:46). A church teacher’s authority is borrowed, which makes the greater strictness fair: he handles words that are not his, about a Lord who will ask how he handled them.

I teach Sunday school, lead a small group, or teach my children. Should this verse frighten me off? It should sober you, not silence you. If God has given you the opportunity and the church has entrusted it to you, do it gladly; parents are commanded to teach their children (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). The warning is for the person who wants the platform more than the people, and for anyone careless with God’s truth. So prepare properly, teach only what Scripture says, admit what you do not know, live what you teach, and let your church’s elders correct you. The Lord who will judge teachers is also the one who forgives them.

How should I choose whom to listen to, especially online? Not every confident voice is a qualified one. Ask: does this teacher explain the Bible, or use it for his own ideas? Is his life consistent with his teaching? Is he accountable to a local church and its elders? Does his teaching make Christ great and make you more humble, holy and loving, or more angry, proud and suspicious? And do not let any online teacher replace the pastor who knows your name and will give account for your soul (Hebrews 13:17).

verseByVerse.quote: For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone stumbles, above all in speech, so a tongue under control is the surest sign of a mature Christian.

We all stumble. To stumble (as in 2:10) is to catch your foot rather than fall headlong. It happens many times, in many areas, to everyone, mostly without intention; and James, a pillar of the Jerusalem church, says “we”.

A perfect man. Perfect means mature, complete (teleios, as in 1:4): not sinlessness but full growth, and the case is hypothetical, since we all stumble. But it gives a practical test. Doctrine, zeal, attendance and even generosity can be produced by effort or temperament; speech is the reliable measure of maturity. The tongue is not the worst part of a person but the controlling part, often the last to come under control, so a man who has it in hand can bridle his whole body.

Why speech tells the truth. Much of what we say is not chosen beforehand, so what comes out when you are tired, interrupted or contradicted is a fair sample of what is inside.

The one perfect man. There has been one such man. “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:22–23). Every word Jesus spoke was true and well timed, all the way to a cross where he said, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). The maturity James describes has a name, and his righteousness, words included, is counted to us who stumble in ours.

What counts as stumbling in speech? More than swearing. Scripture names lying, exaggeration, gossip and slander, flattery, boasting, grumbling, harsh and cutting words, sarcasm meant to wound, crude joking, broken promises and careless words spoken in anger (Ephesians 4:25–31; 5:4; Philippians 2:14). It also includes what we fail to say: the encouragement withheld, the truth not spoken, the apology not made.

In everyday life. Keep a quiet watch on your words for one day, not to scold yourself but to learn. Mark when you exaggerated, interrupted, complained or spoke sharply, and what was happening at the time. At the end of the day confess them specifically, and where someone was hurt, put it right before you sleep. The mouth that never stumbled is speaking for you: he always lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25), and his one word for us outweighs all our careless ones.

Where Christians differ: can a Christian stop stumbling altogether in this life? Some holiness and Wesleyan traditions teach that believers can attain entire sanctification, a state of freedom from conscious sin; they rightly long for a heart wholly given to love, and many of them are earnest, godly people. This commentary’s view: James says we all stumble in many ways, including himself, an apostolic leader. Believers grow in holiness throughout life but are never sinless until glory (1 John 1:8–10; Philippians 3:12–14; Romans 7:14–25). We pursue maturity earnestly, but we always need daily forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Small things steer great ones: the tongue, like a bit or a rudder, sets the course of a whole life. It is not one member among many; it is the helm.

Bits into the mouths of horses. A horse weighs half a ton and can kill a man; the bit is a few ounces of iron, and the disproportion is the whole argument. Control the mouth, control the horse.

The ships also. The same disproportion, with the ship under enormous pressure from the gales; yet a very small rudder, a steering oar at the stern, decides where it goes. Small, and decisive: so is the tongue.

Who has the rudder? The rudder goes wherever the will of the pilot (euthynontos, the one steering) directs: it does not choose its own course. That is the hopeful note in a chapter about to turn very dark. No human being can tame the tongue, but a rudder was never meant to be tamed. It was meant to be steered, and the question is who has hold of it. The winds that drive our lives are strong, but there is a Pilot who has never lost a ship. He who rebuked the wind and calmed the sea (Mark 4:39) can calm the tongue, and bring every one of his people safe into harbour.

A tongue that says Jesus is Lord. The first thing a Christian’s mouth does as a Christian is confess: “if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9). And no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). The rudder has changed hands. A tongue that has once said Jesus is Lord is meant to go on saying it in every sentence after.

In everyday life. Your words are steering your closest relationships toward warmth or toward distance. Choose one relationship where you will deliberately steer with kindness this week.

Does this mean I can steer my life by speaking positive words over it? No. Some teachers claim that our words have creative power, so that by declaring health or wealth we bring it into being. That is not what James means, and it is not biblical: only God speaks things into existence. Our words steer our relationships and our character. A habit of complaining steers a life toward bitterness, a habit of lying toward ruin, a habit of encouragement and prayer toward peace. Our words do not command God; they reveal and shape us.

verseByVerse.quote: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tongue is a fire: one small spark of speech can do vast damage, and its flame is lit from hell. James moves from the tongue’s power to its danger, and every image from here on is destructive.

Yet it boasts of great things. The tongue makes large claims for itself, and it is not bluffing: small as it is, it really can do great things, for good or ill.

Such a small fire. The bit and the rudder were neutral; a fire is not. A spark, and a hillside of brushwood is gone. A single careless word can destroy a reputation, a friendship, a marriage, a church.

A world of unrighteousness. Verse 6 is ferocious: a whole universe of wrong in one organ, lies, slander, gossip, flattery, boasting, cursing, false teaching. Staining is the opposite of the unstained of 1:27: what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person (Matthew 15:11, 18). And it sets on fire the entire course of life, the whole round of a person’s existence, alight from end to end.

Set on fire by hell. Hell here is Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final punishment (Mark 9:43–48): the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once defiled by child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31), later a symbol of God’s judgment. Destructive speech has a supply line, and it runs from below, from Satan, the father of lies (John 8:44).

Why James goes so far. Probably because of his readers: poor, scattered and quarrelling (4:1), they seem to have been harmed less by persecution from outside than by what they were saying to each other.

Tongues set on fire from heaven. The gospel names another supply line. At Pentecost divided tongues as of fire rested on the disciples, and out of their mouths came the mighty works of God (Acts 2:3–4, 11). The same Peter who seven weeks earlier had called down curses and sworn that he did not know the man (Mark 14:71) now preached him to thousands. A tongue lit from hell is not put out by effort. It is relit from above by the ascended Christ, so that tongues which once spread poison might spend eternity in praise.

What it does not mean. Not that the tongue can only do evil: “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21). Nor that the Valley of Hinnom is itself the place of final punishment; the valley gave its name to the real, conscious, eternal punishment of the wicked.

In everyday life. Before you post or send a message, ask whether it will light a fire, and whether you would say it to the person’s face with Christ standing beside you.

When I lose my temper and say terrible things, is that the devil? It is your own sin, for which you are responsible, and the devil is glad to fan it. James does not say every harsh word is demonic possession; he says destructive speech serves the devil’s purposes and draws on his fire. So run to Christ, who has defeated the devil (Hebrews 2:14): hell’s fire is fought not with willpower but with confession, the word of God and the Spirit’s help.

I have already started a fire with my words. What do I do? Act quickly, because fires spread. Go to the person you hurt, privately, and say plainly what you said and that it was wrong, without excuses. If you spread gossip, go back to those you told and correct it. Ask forgiveness from God and from them, and do what you can to restore the reputation you damaged. You cannot unsay words, but honest repentance can stop a fire spreading, and God can rebuild what our tongues have destroyed.

Uncertain wording. Verse 6 is one of the hardest sentences in James to construe, and translations punctuate it differently; the sense is clear, but exactly how the phrases fit together is not. “The entire course of life” is literally “the wheel of birth” (or “of existence”), an unusual phrase found in Greek religious and philosophical writing, perhaps used here as a popular expression. Whether James means the span of a life from birth onward or the whole round of human existence is uncertain; either way, the tongue’s fire reaches everything. In verse 5 the word translated “forest” can also mean brushwood or timber, which does not change the picture.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here translates Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Man has tamed every kind of creature, but no human being can tame his own tongue: it is restless and full of poison.

Every kind of beast and bird. The four kinds of creature echo Genesis 1:26 and 9:2: the rule over the animals that God gave to Adam has actually been carried out.

No human being can tame. The sentence the chapter has been building toward: man rules the animal creation and cannot rule six inches of his own mouth. The claim is absolute and should not be softened into “it is difficult”. It cannot be done, not by resolve, technique or the wisdom of a long life. Only God can (Proverbs 16:1).

A restless evil, full of deadly poison. Restless is the word used of the double-minded man in 1:8: a wild animal pacing in a cage, always ready to break out. The poison is the snake’s: the poison of asps is under their lips (Psalm 140:3; Romans 3:13). A snake is rarely tamed; at best its venom is drawn. And the tongue is not occasionally venomous but full of it.

Why James shuts the door. James deliberately shuts the door on self-improvement. His answer, when it comes at verse 17, is not a technique for controlling speech but a wisdom from above. The problem is not the mouth. It never was.

But we see Jesus. Psalm 8:6–8 celebrates man’s dominion over beasts, birds and fish, and Hebrews, reading it, admits the gap: we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see Jesus, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:8–9). No human being can tame the tongue, but the Son of God became a human being and did. He who spoke the stars into being learned to speak as a child in Nazareth, and never once let poison pass his lips. The dominion lost in Adam is recovered in one man, who ruled his own tongue perfectly and rules ours now by his Spirit.

If no one can tame the tongue, what can a Christian do? God can change the heart from which words come (Matthew 12:34; on how the spring changes, see vv. 11–12). Pray: “Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth” (Psalm 141:3); think before speaking; and when the tongue fails, confess and make it right. The Spirit’s fruit includes self-control (Galatians 5:23).

If I cannot tame my tongue, how can God blame me for what it says? Because the inability is not like a broken leg; it is in the will. Nobody forces the cutting remark out of us. We say it because, at that moment, we want to: the words come up from what the heart loves (3:11; Matthew 12:34). A man who cannot stop lying because he loves himself more than the truth is not less guilty for it, but more. So the answer is not an excuse but a new heart, and the holy God who holds us responsible is also the God who gives the Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

What if someone’s words have poisoned me, and I still hear them years later? Poisonous words from a parent, a spouse, a teacher or a church leader can do deep harm, and this whole passage takes that seriously. Bring those words to God and set them beside what he says about you in Christ: chosen, forgiven, loved, his child. Let his word answer theirs, again and again, until his voice is louder. Talk to a wise pastor or a biblical counsellor if the wound is deep. And if the person is still harming you with words, that is not something you must simply endure; seek help and protection.

verseByVerse.quote: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same mouth that praises God curses the people made in his likeness, and that contradiction ought not to be.

We bless our Lord and Father. This is the double-mindedness of 1:8 in its most visible form, and the pronoun once more is “we”. The blessing is genuine; the same mouth was singing an hour ago. James is describing not hypocrites who despise God, but worshippers.

What it means to bless God. God lacks nothing, so to bless him is to speak well of him, to him and before others. And we never bless him first. He “has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing” (Ephesians 1:3), and “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The curse we deserved fell on Christ so that blessing could come to us, which is why blessing God and cursing people cannot share one mouth: a tongue that has received blessing in place of a curse is meant to pass it on, even to those who curse it (Luke 6:28).

The likeness of God. To curse is to call down evil on someone. The argument turns on “made in the likeness of God”; the Greek tense means made so, and still bearing it. James reaches back to Genesis 1:26–27: cursing a person is an offence against God, not merely an unkind act. Every person was made to reflect him: to know and love him, to think, choose and create, and to look after his world on his behalf (Genesis 1:26–28), rather as a king’s statue in a distant province shows whose land it is. Sin has defaced that likeness but never erased it (Genesis 9:6), so the man you are tempted to curse still carries, however dimly, the marks of his Maker.

The original and the image. You cannot bless the original and curse the image; one of the two acts must be insincere (compare 1 John 4:20). And James does not say we curse our enemies, or the wicked, but “people”: the difficult neighbour, the political opponent, the person in the congregation who has genuinely wronged you.

These things ought not to be so. A remarkably restrained conclusion after the fire of verse 6, and addressed to brothers. It is a real rebuke, for this double-tongued behaviour is incompatible with genuine faith. But James thunders about the tongue in the abstract and speaks softly to the people who have one.

The Image they cursed. The argument reaches its sharpest point at the cross. Every person bears God’s likeness, but one man is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), and men cursed him to his face. Those who passed by derided him, and the chief priests and scribes, men who blessed God in their prayers, mocked him as he died (Mark 15:29–32). Every contemptuous word about a person made in God’s likeness is a small echo of that afternoon.

In everyday life. Let what you sing on Sunday set the tone for how you speak of the difficult colleague on Monday. Take the person you have spoken of most harshly this month and bring them before God: ask him to bless them, and then say one true and good thing about them to someone else.

Is all cursing forbidden, then? The psalms and prophets call down God’s judgment on his enemies, and Paul says a false gospel is accursed (Galatians 1:8); that is leaving judgment to God. What James forbids is cursing people out of malice in our own name; Jesus calls his disciples to “bless those who curse you” (Luke 6:28).

What about swearing and crude language? “Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up” (Ephesians 4:29); filthiness, foolish talk and crude joking are ruled out (Ephesians 5:4). Using God’s name carelessly breaks the third commandment, and obscene speech cheapens what God made good. But the deeper issue James raises is not vocabulary but contempt. A man can avoid every rude word and still destroy someone with a polite sentence. Watch both.

Can I criticise politicians and public figures? Yes: you may disagree with their policies and actions, even strongly, and speak truthfully about wrongdoing. But they too bear God’s image, and we are to pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and honour everyone (1 Peter 2:17). Mockery, slander, half-truths and wishing them harm are what James forbids. A useful test: would you be comfortable if they heard what you said, and if Christ heard it too?

Textual note. “Lord and Father” together is found only here in the New Testament; most later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “God, even the Father”.

verseByVerse.quote: Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What comes out shows what is inside: a spring, a tree or a salt pond gives only what its source supplies, and so does a mouth.

Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Three questions from nature, each expecting the answer no. A spring (pēgē) in dry Palestine was precious, and around the Dead Sea and the Jordan valley sweet springs and brackish ones lie near each other, and no one confuses them. What comes out of a spring’s opening (opē, crack, hole) is determined by what it draws from.

Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives? Each plant produces according to its kind (Genesis 1:11–12). The fig, the olive and the vine were the familiar trees of every village. The Lord had made the identical point: you will recognise them by their fruits; are grapes gathered from thornbushes? (Matthew 7:16–20; 12:33–35).

A salt pond. The final line rules out any softer reading. A salt spring like those near the Dead Sea could not produce drinkable water, not even occasionally. A spring that gives both kinds is not merely inconsistent but impossible; when blessing and cursing come from one mouth, something is wrong at the source.

Deal with the spring. All three pictures say that the output reveals the source, and no tree or spring has ever been talked into producing something foreign to it. So if no human can tame the tongue, what is to be done? You do not work on the water. You deal with the spring. Speech is a symptom.

A new spring. Jesus made the same diagnosis: make the tree good and its fruit good, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:33–34). And he did more than diagnose. To a Samaritan woman he promised water that will become in him “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14), and at the feast he cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink”, speaking, John explains, of the Spirit (John 7:37–39). The source can be changed, and he is the one who changes it.

What it does not mean. Not that a believer who sometimes speaks sinfully is no believer: we all stumble (v. 2). The pattern of our speech reveals the nature of our heart (Luke 6:45). A heart renewed by God will increasingly produce good speech; persistent evil speech reveals an unrenewed heart.

So how does the spring actually change? Only God can change a heart, and he does it through the gospel and his Spirit. In practice that means feeding the spring: filling your mind with Scripture, so that his words are what flow out (Colossians 3:16); confessing the bitterness, envy or fear underneath the words, not just the words themselves; and praying for a clean heart (Psalm 51:10). Behind your harshest words there is usually pride, hurt or fear. Take that to Christ. Sweet water comes from a heart that has been forgiven much and knows it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: True wisdom shows itself in a meek and peaceable life, and it is a gift from above. James tests the claim to be wise by conduct and meekness (v. 13). Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition are a counterfeit wisdom, earthly, unspiritual and demonic, and they leave disorder and every vile practice behind them (vv. 14–16). The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, merciful, impartial and sincere (v. 17), and those who make peace sow a harvest of righteousness (v. 18). This is James’s answer to the untameable tongue: not a technique, but a new source.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wisdom Shown, Not Stated

Wisdom is proved by good conduct in meekness (see the note on v. 13). The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable (see the note on vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition lay behind the quarrelling (see vv. 14–16).

Now: The eagerness to be seen as wise tells against the claim (see the note on v. 13).

verseByVerse.quote: Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Real wisdom proves itself not in talk but in a good life, lived with humble gentleness. The man who must be seen as wise has already shown that he is not.

Who is wise and understanding among you? The question returns to the would-be teachers of verse 1, and tests their claim. Wise (sophos) means having practical, godly wisdom; understanding (epistēmōn) means knowledgeable, expert, skilful.

By his good conduct. Not by an examination or fluency: good conduct is literally a beautiful way of life. Wisdom in the Bible is skill in living, so the evidence for it is a life rather than an argument. A man may explain wisdom faultlessly and not have any.

The meekness of wisdom. This is the phrase that stings. Meekness, as in 1:21, is not timidity but strength under control: a word Greek writers are said to have used of a tamed horse, all its power still there and now answering the rein. The genuinely wise man does not need to win the room or be recognised as the wisest person in it. In a congregation where too many wanted to teach, the eagerness to be seen as wise was itself evidence against the claim.

Learn from me. This is the quality Jesus claimed for himself: “learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The school of heavenly wisdom has one master, and its first lesson is his meekness. The eager would-be teacher is not yet wise because he has not sat at the feet of the gentle one long enough to stop pushing.

Treasures spent on fishermen. The wisest man who ever lived was meek. One greater than Solomon came (Matthew 12:42), and he showed his wisdom not by dazzling the learned but by washing feet. He confounded the scholars at twelve and spent the next years in a carpenter’s shop. He could silence his enemies with a sentence, and he did not open his mouth before his accusers. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), and he spent them on fishermen.

In everyday life. In your next disagreement, at home, at work or in church, be the one who asks questions and listens, and does not need to have the last word.

How can I tell whether a church leader or teacher is truly wise? Look at the life, not only the gifts. Is he humble and teachable? Does he listen before he speaks? How does he treat people who cannot help him: the elderly, children, the awkward, the critic? Is his home in order? How does he handle being contradicted? Paul’s qualifications for elders are mostly about character, not ability (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). A brilliant speaker who is harsh, proud and quarrelsome is not wise, however impressive he sounds.

Isn’t meekness just weakness? Not in Scripture. Moses confronted Pharaoh and was called the meekest man on earth. Jesus overturned the money-changers’ tables and called himself gentle and lowly. Meekness is power yielded to God: strong enough to fight, humble enough not to fight for itself. The meek can stand firm on the truth and still be gentle in manner, be wronged without retaliating, and lose an argument without losing their peace. That takes more strength, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Envy and selfish ambition dressed up as wisdom come from below, not from above, and they tear a church apart. James has found the spring behind the quarrelling tongues.

Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition. Jealousy is zēlos, zeal, which can be a virtue and here is bitter, like the salt water of verse 11: passion for a cause curdled into passion against a person. Selfish ambition is a rare word used before the New Testament of self-seeking in politics: working a crowd for your own advancement.

In your hearts. This is the spring of verse 11. To claim to be wise while this is going on inside you is not merely mistaken: it is to be false to the truth, a lie told about reality.

Earthly, unspiritual, demonic. The verdict, in three descending words. Earthly: it belongs to this world and reaches no higher. Unspiritual, literally soulish: merely human powers of mind and feeling, working without the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:14; Jude 19). Demonic, where the descent ends: its ultimate source is the devil, whose original sin Scripture links with pride (1 Timothy 3:6).

Disorder and every vile practice. Disorder is upheaval, confusion, the same word family as the restless tongue of verse 8 and the unstable man of 1:8. Private ambition produces public chaos, and the chaos makes room for everything else.

The wisdom that crucified the Lord of glory. James’s analysis was once proved on a public scale. Pilate knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up (Matthew 27:18). Fear for their place became a plot (John 11:48), the plot a trial with false witnesses, the trial a crowd demanding a murderer’s release. None of the rulers of this age understood God’s wisdom, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). Selfish ambition sat among his own disciples at the Last Supper, arguing about which of them was the greatest, and the one with every right to ambition answered it by taking a towel, and then a cross. That earthly, unspiritual, demonic wisdom killed Christ, and God turned its worst act into the salvation of the world.

What it does not mean. It does not condemn all ambition. Wanting to serve God well and use our gifts fully is good: “earnestly desire the higher gifts” (1 Corinthians 12:31), and “If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task” (1 Timothy 3:1). James condemns selfish ambition, which seeks its own glory at others’ expense.

How do I fight envy when a friend succeeds where I have not? Name it honestly before God; envy hides behind criticism and loves to call itself discernment. Your worth is set not by comparison but by God’s love for you in Christ, and he gives his gifts as he wills. Then do the opposite of what envy wants: thank God for your friend’s blessing, pray for them, and tell them you are glad. “Rejoice with those who rejoice” (Romans 12:15). Feelings often follow obedience. And look at what God has given you; envy blinds us to our own gifts.

Our church is in conflict, and I think ambition is behind it. What should I do? Start with your own heart: is there any selfish ambition or bitterness in you? Then refuse to feed the fire: do not gossip, take sides on social media, or spread rumours. Take any concern privately and humbly to the person or to the elders (Matthew 18:15). Pray for the leaders and for peace. Be a peacemaker, not a party member. If there is real sin or abuse, it must be dealt with properly and openly, not covered up. Truth and peace together are the goal.

verseByVerse.quote: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisdom God gives is first pure and then peace-loving, and those who live by it sow peace that grows into a harvest of righteousness. This is the answer to the whole chapter: not a technique for controlling the tongue, which cannot be done, but a wisdom given to anyone who asks (1:5).

First pure. This wisdom comes from the same direction as every good gift (1:17): it is not achieved but given. First means first in priority, the foundation of the rest. Pure means holy, without mixed motives.

Then peaceable. Purity comes before peaceableness, which forbids the false peace that keeps quiet about sin to avoid trouble. But with that order secured, peace governs everything after it, the opposite of the jealousy and disorder of verses 14–16.

Gentle, open to reason. Gentle (epieikēs, almost untranslatable) is gracious, considerate, forbearing: the man who does not insist on the last inch of his rights, a qualification for elders (1 Timothy 3:3). Open to reason is easily persuaded, willing to yield, teachable: an extraordinary thing to require of wisdom, and exactly what the quarrelling teachers lacked.

Full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. Mercy is compassion in action, as in 2:13, and good fruits are the works that show faith is alive (2:14–26). Impartial is undivided, unprejudiced, reaching back both to the gold ring of 2:1–9 and to the double-minded man of 1:6–8. Sincere is without a mask, not play-acting: the opposite of the double-mindedness that runs through the whole letter.

A harvest of righteousness. The chapter that opened with fire closes with sowing. Fire destroys in an afternoon; sowing produces slowly, and only in the right conditions. Peacemakers do not merely avoid conflict; they make peace, which is work, and which is what the whole congregation had stopped doing. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

What the list leaves out. Not one of these qualities is about cleverness: heavenly wisdom is described almost entirely by how a person treats others. And read with Jesus in view, the list is a portrait, for he became to us wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:30). Pure: he knew no sin. Gentle: a bruised reed he did not break. Open to reason: he answered honest questions patiently, from Nicodemus by night to doubting Thomas. Full of mercy and good fruits: he went about doing good. Impartial: he ate with Pharisees and with tax collectors. Sincere: no deceit was found in his mouth. The wisdom from above has a face.

The wisdom from above came down. It lay in a manger and hung on a cross, and there the great Peacemaker made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), sown in the ground like a seed so that a harvest of righteousness could rise from his grave. He is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), and the wisdom that came down is still given to everyone who asks.

In everyday life. Go down the list, pick the quality you most lack, and ask God for it, as he promised (1:5).

Does open to reason mean I should change my convictions whenever someone disagrees? No. Wisdom is first pure; it does not bend on what God has clearly said. But on everything else, and on how we hold what God has said, it is willing to listen, to learn and to admit error. The wise person can say, “I had not thought of that; you may be right; I was wrong.” The foolish person cannot. If you hold your own opinions as firmly as you hold God’s word, you have probably confused the two.

How do I actually make peace? Begin by being at peace with God through Christ, because peacemakers are those who have been reconciled (Romans 5:1). Then go first: do not wait for the other person to come to you (Matthew 5:23–24). Listen to understand, not to win. Own your part honestly, without adding “but”. Speak the truth gently. Look for what you can agree on. If two other believers are in conflict, do not carry stories between them; help them talk to each other, or bring in a wise elder. And keep sowing: peace often grows slowly, like a harvest.
