keyVerse.quote: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.
keyVerse.note: This is James’s answer to the problem the chapter has laid bare. If no human being can tame the tongue (v. 8), the cure must come from outside us, and it does: a wisdom from above, given to those who ask (1:5). Almost every quality in the list concerns how we treat other people, and together they draw a portrait of Christ himself.

3.reflection:
James says that the person who does not stumble in what he says is “a perfect man” (v. 2). Why is speech such a reliable test of maturity? What does your own speech tend to show when you are tired, interrupted or contradicted?

Verses 9–10 say we bless God and curse people made in his likeness. Whom do you find it hardest to speak well of, and how does remembering that they bear God’s image change the way you speak about them?

James moves from the tongue to the heart: a spring gives only what its source supplies (vv. 11–12). If words cannot be tamed by effort, how does the source actually change? What part do Scripture, confession and prayer play?

Read the list in verse 17 slowly. Which quality do you most lack, and where could you be a peacemaker (v. 18) this week, at home, at work or in this church?

4.title: Submit to God: Pride, the World, and the Brevity of Life
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 traced the quarrelling tongue to envy and selfish ambition in the heart (3:14–16). Chapter 4 follows the trail down to its root, and then exposes two more faces of the same pride.

The message. Your fights with one another come from a war inside you: desires that grab instead of asking God. That love of the world is adultery against the God who loves you jealously, and he opposes the proud. But he gives more grace. So come to him low: submit, resist the devil, draw near, wash, grieve over your sin, and he will lift you up. And stop taking his place, whether by sitting in judgment on a brother or by treating tomorrow as your own.

Why it was said. Scattered, poor and hard-pressed (see the introduction), these believers were turning on one another: quarrelling, coveting and slandering, while some, perhaps the traders among them, planned the year’s profit without a thought of God (v. 13). James writes as a pastor who will not let a church treat its feuds as mere differences of opinion.

How the chapter makes its case. First the diagnosis (vv. 1–3): quarrels come from passions at war within, which grab rather than ask, or ask only to feed themselves. Then the name for it (vv. 4–5): friendship with the world is spiritual adultery, and God yearns jealously over his people. Then the turn on which the chapter hangs (v. 6): “But he gives more grace”, to the humble. Ten urgent commands spell out what it is to come to God low (vv. 7–10), ending with the promise that he will exalt the humble. Two more forms of pride follow, each taking God’s place: slander, which climbs into the seat of the one Lawgiver and Judge (vv. 11–12), and the confident plan that forgets that life is a mist (vv. 13–16). Verse 17 seals it: to know the good and leave it undone is sin.

Where it leads. The chapter is a mirror held up to Christ. Where we grasp, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped; where we are divided, he desired one thing above all, his Father’s will. The God we betrayed is the husband who buys back his unfaithful bride, and the “more grace” of verse 6 is spoken in a human voice by the one who is “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). He was humbled so that we could be lifted up. The one Judge died for the people we condemn, and the only man who always did the good he knew gave himself for our tomorrows.

For us. Name the desire under your last quarrel and bring it to God instead of fighting for it. Bring the sin you are most ashamed of, and hear “he gives more grace”. And learn to say, and mean, “If the Lord wills.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Quarrels, Adultery, and More Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Our fights come from a heart that loves the world, yet God meets even that with more grace. James traces the quarrels to passions at war within, which grab instead of asking God, or ask only to feed themselves (vv. 1–3). Such love of the world is adultery against the God who yearns jealously over his people (vv. 4–5). But he gives more grace, to the humble (v. 6), and ten urgent commands spell out what it is to come to him low: submit, resist, draw near, cleanse, purify, grieve and humble yourselves, with the promise that he will lift you up (vv. 7–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
But He Gives More Grace

Quarrels come from desires at war within us (see vv. 1–2), and friendship with the world is spiritual adultery (see v. 4). Yet God gives more grace to the humble (see the note on vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers prayed, but to fund their desires (see the note on v. 3).

Now: Submit to God, resist the devil, draw near, and he will draw near to you (see vv. 7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our quarrels with one another come from a war inside us: desires that grab what they want instead of asking God for it.

What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? James asks it as a doctor asks where the pain is. Quarrels (polemoi, wars) and fights (machai, battles) are military words for church conflicts. Chapter 3 traced the quarrelling tongues to jealousy and selfish ambition (3:14–16); now he goes deeper still.

Your passions are at war within you. Passions are desires for pleasure (hēdonai, from which we get hedonism). At war (strateuomenōn) means waging a military campaign, and the battlefield is “within you”, literally “in your members”, the parts of your own body. The war is first not between factions but within each person, where desires fight against God and each other (Romans 7:23; 1 Peter 2:11).

The quarrel is only the symptom. A man at war inside will find something to fight about outside; settle one question and he will find another. The music, the building, the rota, the budget: these are rarely the real war. They are only where it broke out.

So you murder. Verse 2 packs a great deal into few words. James is probably doing what his brother did in the Sermon on the Mount: tracing sin to its root, where hatred is already murder (Matthew 5:21–22; 1 John 3:15). He is not accusing them of homicide but naming where the desire is heading: hatred, character assassination, destroying others with words, as unchecked desire led Cain (see “Uncertain wording” below).

You covet. The pattern comes twice: desire, frustration, violence. The violence is not the root problem; it is what desire does when it is blocked.

Because you do not ask. After all that heat, the simplest sentence. They have organised their whole inner life around getting, and it has not occurred to them to ask the God who gives generously to all without reproach (1:5). We try to grab what God would give if we asked.

Grasping or asking. Behind the quarrel lies a lie about God: that what he withholds must be seized. James answers it with the teaching of Jesus: “Ask, and it will be given to you”, and “how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:7–11). And Jesus lived it. Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6); and the Father’s word to him was, “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8). The church fights because it grasps; its Lord, who alone had the right to take, asked. In him there was no war within: he desired his Father’s will above all, and every other desire was ordered under it. The war inside us will not end by our own resolve. It ends at the feet of the Prince of Peace.

Where do our wars really come from? The modern instinct is to look for the cause of conflict outside us: scarcity, bad systems, poor education, the people on the other side. James points somewhere less comfortable. The French thinker René Girard spent much of his life on a related insight: we learn what to want by watching what others want, so our desires converge on the same objects, and the person we copy becomes our rival; a screen showing everyone else’s life all day is a machine for exactly that. Augustine had noticed long before that the goods of this world divide those who share them: the more of the house, the honour or the spotlight you have, the less there is for me. God is the one good not lessened by being shared, which is why asking him ends the war. Christ, who could have grasped everything, gave himself away, and those who have him are no longer competing for the one thing they most need.

What it does not mean. Not that all desire is wrong: “Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 37:4). The problem is desire for pleasure that rules us and sets us against others.

In everyday life. Underneath your last argument, at home, at work or in church, what did you want: respect, control, comfort, to be right, to be noticed? Name the desire, and bring it to God in prayer instead of fighting for it.

But surely some church conflicts are about real issues, like truth? Yes. Some disagreements are about the gospel itself, and then faithfulness requires standing firm (Jude 3; Galatians 2:11). But even then James’s question is worth asking: what is going on in me? It is possible to be right about the issue and wrong in the heart, fighting for truth with pride, anger and a desire to win. And most church quarrels, honestly examined, are not about the gospel at all but about preferences, status and being heard. Ask God to show you which yours is.

Does “you do not ask” mean that if I pray I will get whatever I want? No; the next verse rules that out. James means that many of our battles would end if we took our desires to God instead of fighting for them. When we bring a desire to God honestly, he gives it, or gives something better, or changes the desire. All three end the war inside. Grabbing never does.

Uncertain wording. The punctuation of verse 2 is debated: the ESV pairs desire with murder and coveting with fighting, while some translations join the clauses differently. Because “murder” seems so strong, some have suggested that James really wrote the similar-looking Greek word for “envy”, but the manuscripts do not support it. The ESV’s reading, taken as the language of Jesus about hatred, makes good sense.

verseByVerse.quote: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even when they pray, they ask with the wrong motive, to feed their own appetites, so God in kindness says no.

You ask wrongly. James anticipates the protest, “But I have asked.” The fault is not in the asking but in the motive. To spend is the verb used of the prodigal son spending everything in the far country (Luke 15:14), and “passions” is the same word, pleasures, as in verse 1.

A kind refusal. These people have not abandoned prayer. They have turned it into a way of funding the very appetites that are tearing the congregation apart, and God, mercifully, declines. A father who financed every appetite his children presented would not be generous but negligent.

What would I do with it? When a prayer has gone unanswered for years, the honest question is not only “Why is God silent?” but “What would I do with it if I got it?” James does not put that question to someone asking for a real need; he has just told them to ask. He puts it to our wants.

The Son was refused. When his own Son prayed, “let this cup pass from me”, the answer was no, so that every prayer of his people might be heard for his sake. The Son was refused so that we could be received. He always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25), and he takes our muddled prayers, cleanses them, and presents them to the Father as his own.

What it does not mean. Not that we may never pray for good things for ourselves: Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread (Matthew 6:11). We ask according to his will (1 John 5:14), not merely for our own pleasure.

How do I know whether my motives are right? Ask what you want the thing for. If God gave it, would it draw you closer to him or make you need him less? Would it serve others, or only you? Could you pray “your will be done” and mean it? Motives are rarely pure, so do not wait for perfect ones: bring the mixture to God and ask him to purify it. Praying honestly is one of the ways he changes our motives.

I have prayed for years for something good: a child’s salvation, healing, a marriage. Are my motives wrong? Not necessarily. James is speaking about prayers to fund selfish pleasure, not prayers for the good of others or for God’s glory. Many faithful prayers are answered slowly, or in ways we do not see, or not in this life; Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac. Keep praying: Jesus told a parable so that we would always pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). Unanswered prayer is a reason to examine your heart, but also a call to trust the wisdom of a Father who knows what you do not.

verseByVerse.quote: You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To love the world is to be unfaithful to God, like an adulterous wife, and it makes us his enemies.

You adulterous people! The Greek is feminine, adulteresses (moichalides), and it is not an insult about women. It is the prophets’ language, in which Israel is the bride and idolatry is infidelity (Hosea 1–3), and the church is the bride of Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). To love the world is to cheat on God. That reframes the whole chapter: the quarrelling, the coveting and the misdirected prayers are not merely bad behaviour. They are a marriage being broken.

Friendship with the world is enmity with God. Friendship means affection and shared outlook. The world is not the planet or the people in it, but human society organised apart from and against God, with its values of pride, greed, pleasure and self (1:27; 1 John 2:15–17). Enmity (echthra) is hostility. The claim is deliberately stark: friendship with the world does not lead to enmity, or risk it; it is enmity. You cannot be friends with both.

Whoever wishes. The warning is not about living in the world or enjoying good things; the God of this letter gives every good gift (1:17). It is about where the affections are pointed: the wishing is the adultery. And “makes himself” means he does it to himself. God has not declared war on him; he has taken up a position against God. That is why the next verses can still offer him grace and not a sentence.

A husband who does not give up. The God we betrayed does not abandon his bride. When Israel played the harlot, he sent Hosea to buy back his unfaithful wife, and said, “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hosea 2:19). We are the adulteress whom Christ has redeemed and is making pure, and his faithfulness is greater than our unfaithfulness.

Enemies made friends. How does an enemy become a friend again? While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). The one who was mocked as a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11:19) laid down his life for them, and then said to his disciples, “I have called you friends” (John 15:15). That friendship is what breaks the world’s hold, because it is better than anything the world can offer.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should hate the people of the world. God loves the world of people (John 3:16), and we are sent into it (John 17:15–18).

What counts as worldliness? Is it films, clothes, music? Worldliness is less about particular things than about the heart’s loyalty. John defines it as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and pride of life (1 John 2:16): wanting what pleases the body, what looks good, and what makes us important. A Christian can avoid every questionable film and still be thoroughly worldly in his love of money or status. Ask: where do I get my sense of worth? Whose approval do I most want? What would I be most devastated to lose? If the answer is anything other than God, that is where the world has your heart.

Can a Christian become an enemy of God? James writes to church members, and the warning is real. A professing Christian who settles into love of the world shows that his heart is drifting from God, and if he persists without repentance, he shows that his profession was never genuine (1 John 2:19). But a true believer who has strayed will be drawn back; God disciplines his children and does not let them go (Hebrews 12:6; John 10:28). The very next verses are the way back: “he gives more grace”. If you are troubled by your worldliness, that trouble is his jealous love calling you home.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “adulterers and adulteresses”; the earliest have only the feminine.
verseByVerse.note: The prophets called Israel’s unfaithfulness to God “adultery.”

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us”? But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
God loves his people with a jealous love and will not share them with the world, yet to the humble he gives grace greater than all their unfaithfulness. Verse 6 is the hinge of the chapter.

He yearns jealously. However the hard details are settled (see “Uncertain wording” below), the plain point is not in doubt: God loves his people with a jealous love and wants them wholly for himself. Scripture does not say so in vain; it is a warning to the double-minded.

But he gives more grace. After the severity of verses 1–5, verse 6 arrives like a door opening. More grace: greater than the adultery, the quarrelling, and the appetite that has been running the congregation. Grace is favour no one has earned, given where judgment was due, and with it his power to change us (Titus 2:11–12). When we have exhausted our resolutions, he gives more. When we have betrayed him again, he gives more. God’s demand is total, but his grace is greater, enough for every failure and every temptation: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

God opposes the proud. The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, and it names the one condition. Grace is not scarce, but it flows downhill, and it will not reach a man who has set himself above it. “Opposes” is a military word: to line up in battle array against. God does not merely withhold from the proud; he opposes them.

Lowly in heart. Grace collects in the low places, and the Son of God went there first. Jesus described himself with James’s own word for the humble (tapeinos): “I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). In his Son God came down to where the humble are, and his call to the weary and heavy laden is the “more grace” of verse 6, spoken in a human voice. To humble yourself is not to earn grace; it is to come to the low place where Christ is already standing.

In everyday life. Bring to mind the sin you are most ashamed of, the one you feel has used up God’s patience. Read these four words again: “he gives more grace”. Then do the humble thing: confess it plainly, without excuses, and receive the grace. It is not a reservoir that runs low; from his fullness we have all received grace upon grace (John 1:16).

How can God be jealous, if jealousy is a sin? Jealousy is sinful when it wants what is not ours, or resents another’s good. But there is a right jealousy, for what truly belongs to us: a husband who did not care if his wife loved another man would not be admirable. God’s jealousy is his holy, protective love for those who are his by creation and redemption. He is jealous for us, not of us; he wants our whole heart because he is our true good, and anything else we give it to will destroy us. His name is Jealous (Exodus 34:14), and it is a name of love.

How do I become humble? Not by trying to feel small, or by putting yourself down, which is often pride in disguise. Humility grows by looking at God, his holiness, greatness and grace: Isaiah saw the Lord and said, “Woe is me!” (Isaiah 6:5). It grows at the cross, where we see what our sin cost and what we were given freely. And it shows itself in practice: admitting you are wrong, asking for help, serving where no one sees, rejoicing in others’ success, receiving correction without defending yourself. Humility is not thinking less of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less, because you are thinking of him.

Uncertain wording. Verse 5 is the hardest sentence in the letter to translate, and it is better to say so than to pretend to be sure. The Greek can be read in three main ways, and the ESV margin notes the others: God yearns jealously over the human spirit he breathed into us at creation (Genesis 2:7), the ESV’s reading; God yearns jealously for the Holy Spirit he made to dwell in believers; or the human spirit God made to dwell in us longs enviously, a charge against sinful desire (the KJV’s reading: “the spirit that dwelleth in us lusteth to envy”). Nor does any Old Testament verse say it in these words; James seems to sum up Scripture’s teaching on God’s jealousy (Exodus 20:5; 34:14; Deuteronomy 32:16; Zechariah 8:2). The first reading fits the context of divided loyalty best: God will not share us with the world.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 5 is hard to translate; the ESV margin offers other readings. No single Old Testament verse matches it; it seems to sum up Scripture’s teaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coming to God humbly means submitting to him, resisting the devil and drawing near with clean hands and an undivided heart, and God promises to meet us. The ten commands of verses 7–10 unpack one word from verse 6: the humble.

Submit yourselves therefore to God. “Submit” is military again: arrange yourself under, like soldiers under a commander. It is the opposite of the proud man’s posture, and it comes first because everything else follows from it.

What it means to submit to God. Submission sounds to modern ears like losing yourself, the beginning of being crushed. But nobody actually lives unsubmitted. Everyone bows to something, our own appetites, other people’s opinions, the need to stay in control, and those masters are harder than we admit. To submit to God is to stop arguing with him about who is in charge, and to let him have the last word where you and he disagree. Timothy Keller often pointed out that if your God never disagrees with you, you may simply be worshipping an idealised version of yourself.

Resist the devil. The order matters: submit first, then resist; a man who has not submitted to God has no ground to stand on. And the promise is not victory after a long siege but flight. The devil is real and active (1 Peter 5:8–9; Ephesians 6:11–13), but he is a defeated enemy (Hebrews 2:14).

Draw near. This is priestly language, used of approaching the altar (Hebrews 7:19), and James applies it to ordinary believers. God responds to those who come to him (Zechariah 1:3; Malachi 3:7). But he is not waiting at a distance until we have travelled far enough; the chapter has just said he yearns jealously over us and gives more grace. We draw near to a God who is already leaning toward us, like the prodigal’s father, who ran (Luke 15:20). When we take one trembling step toward him, we find he has been running toward us all along, with a robe and a ring and a feast.

Cleanse your hands, purify your hearts. Hands are outward actions; priests washed their hands before approaching God (Exodus 30:19–21). Hearts are inward loyalty, and both are required: “Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD?” “He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:3–4). “Sinners” is a strong word for church members, used deliberately to shock. And “double-minded” is dipsychos again, the “two-souled” word of 1:8: a heart torn between God and the world. Here at last James gives its cure, not trying harder but being made clean, and the command comes only after “he gives more grace”.

Not my will, but yours. Why trust God with the last word? Because submission to the Father has already been walked to the end. In the garden the Son prayed, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42), and his yielding carried him to a cross for us. The God who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32) is not a commander who will use you up and throw you away.

Why the devil runs. The promise that he will flee is astonishing until we ask who has already fought him. Jesus met the devil in the wilderness with nothing but submission to his Father and the written word, and the devil left him (Matthew 4:11). At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). The believer who submits and resists stands inside a victory already won: the devil flees because he has already been beaten by the one the believer belongs to.

What it does not mean. Not that we cleanse ourselves by our own power. Christ’s blood cleanses (1 John 1:7, 9); but we must turn from sin in repentance, by grace.

In everyday life. This week, take one command of Scripture you have been quietly arguing with, and do it, asking God for the grace to mean it. And where is the devil pressing you right now: a lie about God, an accusation, a temptation, a fear? Find one verse that answers the lie directly and say it aloud when the pressure comes.

How does a believer resist the devil? By standing firm in faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), putting on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:11–17), and answering his lies with God’s word, as Jesus did in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11). It does not mean shouting at Satan or using formulas; even the archangel said only, “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 9).

I have tried to draw near, but God still feels far away. What now? Feelings are not the measure of God’s nearness. He has promised to draw near, and he keeps his promises whether you feel it or not. Many saints have known long seasons of dryness; the psalmists cried, “How long?” (Psalm 13:1). Keep doing what draws near: read his word, pray honestly, gather with his people, take the Lord’s Supper, confess known sin. Check for anything you are holding back from him. And rest on the fact that in Christ you have already been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). Your nearness to God rests on Christ’s work, not on your sense of it.

Where Christians differ: does our drawing near come first, then God’s? Some read “draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” as teaching that human initiative comes first and God responds; they rightly hear a real and urgent invitation in it. This commentary’s view: this command is addressed to believers already born again by God’s will (1:18), and James has just said God gives more grace (v. 6). God’s grace always comes first: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). Within a relationship already begun by grace, God calls us to draw near and promises to meet us. Our drawing near is itself the fruit of his drawing us.

verseByVerse.quote: Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take your sin seriously enough to grieve over it, and bow low before the Lord, and he will lift you up. The humbling is ours to do; the exalting is his to give.

Be wretched and mourn and weep. To mourn is to grieve as for the dead; to weep is to cry aloud: deep sorrow over sin (Joel 2:12–13).

Laughter to mourning. James is addressing people who have been quarrelling, coveting and committing spiritual adultery, and doing it cheerfully. The laughter to be turned to mourning is the careless laughter of those who enjoy worldly pleasures without a thought of God (Ecclesiastes 7:2–6). Gloom is dejection, literally downcast eyes: the posture of the tax collector who would not even lift up his eyes to heaven (Luke 18:13).

Godly grief. This is not a call to permanent gloom. There is a grief that is the right response to your own sin, and whoever can look at what James has just described and feel none of it has not understood. Paul calls it godly grief, which produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret (2 Corinthians 7:10). And if you are already low, grieving or depressed, this is not a call to pile more sorrow on yourself: James is speaking to the careless and the cheerfully worldly, and the Lord who says it is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).

He will exalt you. The humbling is commanded, and it is ours; the exalting is promised, and it is his. That is the Bible’s pattern for the whole Christian life, and the exact reverse of what we do by nature: we exalt ourselves and hope God will not humble us (1 Peter 5:6). James does not say humility is its own reward, but that God lifts the person who takes the low place.

Weep now, laugh later. James is again echoing Jesus, who pronounced a blessing on those who weep now, for they shall laugh, and a woe on those who laugh now, for they shall mourn and weep (Luke 6:21, 25). To turn laughter into mourning is to get onto the right side of Christ’s great reversal. The world’s careless laughter ends in tears, and the tears of repentance end in his joy. It is the pattern of his own life (Philippians 2:8–9): he mourned so that we could be comforted; he was humbled so that we could be lifted up.

I feel I can never grieve enough over my sin. How much grief is enough? Godly grief is not measured by quantity of tears, and you do not earn forgiveness by feeling bad enough. Christ’s blood, not your sorrow, pays for sin. Godly grief turns you to God; once it has done that, its work is done, and the next step is to receive forgiveness and be lifted up. If you find yourself endlessly mourning sins already confessed, that is not humility; it is failing to believe the promise (1 John 1:9). Mourn honestly, then let God exalt you. He wants his children forgiven and glad, not perpetually downcast.

Is there a place for this kind of mourning in church life today? Yes, and many churches have lost it. Times of honest confession in worship, days of prayer and humbling when a church has sinned or is in crisis, grief over a nation’s or a family’s sin: these are biblical (Nehemiah 9; Daniel 9). A church that only ever celebrates may be skipping the repentance that makes the celebration real; the joy of the gospel is deepest in those who have felt the weight of their sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride shows two more faces, and both take God’s place. The slanderer climbs into the seat of the one Lawgiver and Judge, condemning the neighbour he was commanded to love (vv. 11–12). The confident planner treats tomorrow as his own, forgetting that his life is a mist, when the humble say, “If the Lord wills” (vv. 13–16). The section ends with a definition of sin as good known and left undone (v. 17), which gathers up the whole letter’s call to be doers and not hearers only.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sin as Knowledge Not Acted On

Speaking against a brother sets us over the law instead of under it. And whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The merchants' plan was complete except for God (see vv. 13–15).

Now: Plan, but hold every plan under “if the Lord wills” (see the note on vv. 13–15).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks evil against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is only one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?
verseByVerse.commentary:
To run down a brother is to climb into God’s seat, for he alone gives the law and judges by it.

Do not speak evil. To talk down, to speak against: slander, criticise, run down. It covers not only lies but any speech that tears another person down behind their back: the tongue of chapter 3 turned on the congregation. The other verb, judges, means condemns, sits in judgment on another’s worth or motives.

Judges the law. The law says love your neighbour as yourself, the royal law of 2:8, and the same paragraph of Leviticus forbids slander (Leviticus 19:16–18). If you set that aside in order to condemn somebody, you have not merely disobeyed it. You have passed judgment on it, ruling that in this case it does not apply, as if you were above it.

Not a doer but a judge. Chapter 1 divided the world into hearers and doers; here it is doers and judges. You cannot be both, because a judge stands over the law and a doer stands under it (1:22–25).

One lawgiver and judge, able to save and to destroy. “For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us” (Isaiah 33:22). God alone gives the law and judges by it, and what qualifies him is that he can carry out the verdict either way. Only God has power over eternal destiny (Matthew 10:28; Deuteronomy 32:39). To judge others is to usurp his place.

But who are you to judge your neighbor? The “you” is emphatic in the Greek (sy de tis ei): you, of all people? It is a real question of authority: the case is not yours to try (Romans 14:4). And the last word is neighbour, which pulls Leviticus 19:18 back into the sentence one final time. The person you are judging is the person you were commanded to love.

The bench belongs to Christ. James is echoing the Lord’s warning against judging, with its speck and its log (Matthew 7:1–5). And the one Lawgiver and Judge has a name. “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), and “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). The slanderer is climbing into Jesus’ seat to pass sentence on someone for whom Jesus died (Romans 14:15), someone who will answer to his own Master, not to us.

In everyday life. The Judge has already borne the sentence your own words deserved, so you need not climb into his seat. This week, refuse to speak negatively about anyone behind their back. If you have a concern, go to them, or to God.

Does this forbid all judging? No. James forbids slander and condemning a brother as if we were his final judge. Scripture still calls us to judge teaching and conduct by God’s word (1 John 4:1), and the church to exercise discipline (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). What is forbidden is taking God’s seat.

If what I say about someone is true, is it still slander? It can be. James’s word covers accurate but damaging talk behind someone’s back. Ask: why am I saying this, and to whom? If you are telling people who have no need to know, in order to lower someone in their eyes, it is sin even if every word is true. Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8). If the matter is serious, go to the person, or to those with responsibility to act. If it is not serious, let it go.

But what if I need to warn others about someone dangerous? That is not slander; it is love for the vulnerable. If someone is abusing, defrauding or endangering others, the truth must be spoken to those who need to know: the authorities, the elders, those at risk. Protecting the weak is commanded (Proverbs 31:8–9), and covering up harm in the name of not judging is itself a grave wrong. Slander wants to damage a reputation; a warning wants to protect people. Speak the facts plainly, to the right people, and leave the final judgment of the heart to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”— yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Planning is not wrong, but planning as if tomorrow were ours forgets that our lives are a passing mist in God’s hand.

Come now. An abrupt call to attention, now addressed to merchants and businesspeople. Travelling trade was a familiar way of life among Jews of the Dispersion, who moved between the cities of the empire to buy and sell (see the introduction), so the scene was one his readers knew, and some probably lived it.

Today or tomorrow. The business plan is entirely reasonable: timing, destination, duration, activity and outcome are all settled. Trade, profit and planning are not condemned; Scripture commends the ant who prepares her bread in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8). What is missing is the clause James supplies in verse 15. There is no thought of God.

You do not know what tomorrow will bring. Not gloom, but fact: the plan assumes knowledge nobody has. “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring” (Proverbs 27:1). Jesus’ rich fool made the same mistake: “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:16–21). Underneath the confident plan there is often a hunger for control: if I can map out tomorrow, I need not trust anyone with it, not even God. The plan becomes a refuge, and James gently takes it away so that the Lord himself can be the refuge (Psalm 46:1).

What is your life? Mist (atmis) is steam, vapour, morning haze: the vapour over a field that is gone once the sun is properly up, like breath on a cold morning or steam from a pot. Not a short life; a brief appearance, here for a moment and then gone (Job 7:7; Psalm 39:5; 102:3; 144:4). Our lives are a mist, but the Lord who holds them is not: “from everlasting to everlasting you are God” (Psalm 90:2). And because Christ gave his life for us, our mist of a life is bound up in his endless one; when the sun rises on the last day, those in him will not vanish but shine.

If the Lord wills. The correction is smaller than we expect. James does not cancel the trip or the trade. He adds a clause, and it covers not only the doing but the living: “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.” Paul used similar words (Acts 18:21). God’s providence governs all things, including our tomorrows.

Tomorrow in the Father’s hand. Behind James stands Jesus’ teaching about tomorrow. He did not cure presumption with anxiety. He told his disciples not to be anxious about tomorrow either, because their heavenly Father knows what they need, and to seek first his kingdom (Matthew 6:32–34). Boasting and worrying make the same mistake: both leave the Father out of tomorrow. “If the Lord wills” is not a shrug. It is the speech of a child who knows whose hands tomorrow is in, and it is Christ who has made us children of that Father.

Is it wrong to save, buy insurance or plan for retirement? No. Scripture commends wise preparation: Joseph stored grain for the famine, and a good man leaves an inheritance (Proverbs 13:22). The question is not whether you plan but in what spirit. Do your savings make you feel independent of God, or are they held as his? Are you storing up for yourself, like the rich fool, or rich toward God? Plan carefully, hold the plan loosely, give generously along the way, and trust him with what you cannot control.

How do I hold my plans loosely without becoming passive or anxious? Plan as wisely as you can, and offer each plan to God in prayer. When plans fail, as many will, receive it as his will rather than as a disaster. “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). This is not fatalism but trust, which frees you both from the anxiety of having to control tomorrow and from the pride of thinking you can. Do your part today, and leave tomorrow to the one who holds it.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boasting about a future we do not control is evil, and knowing the good we should do and not doing it is sin.

You boast in your arrogance. The word for arrogance comes from the Greek figure of the braggart, often pictured as the travelling impostor who claimed powers he did not have. They boast about their plans as if the future were theirs to command: the pride of life (1 John 2:16).

All such boasting is evil. Not unwise or naive, but evil, because it is a claim to a knowledge and control that belong to God alone, made by a mist. It is practical atheism: living as though God did not rule.

Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it. Verse 17 reads like a detached proverb, but the “So” ties it to what goes before. These men now know about the mist and “If the Lord wills”, so their planning can no longer be excused as thoughtlessness. We usually think of sin as doing what is forbidden; James adds that it is also sin not to do what we know is right: a sin of omission, good left undone.

The whole letter in a sentence. The man who hears and does not do is deceiving himself (1:22); the man who says and does not give is useless (2:16); the man who knows and does not act is sinning. James never charges his readers with not knowing, only with knowing and not doing. That is sobering for anyone who hears much and reads much: we answer for more with every sermon understood and every chapter agreed with (Luke 12:47).

Not done to me. Jesus taught the same truth in the starkest terms. In his picture of the last judgment, those on the King’s left are condemned not for crimes they committed but for the hungry they did not feed and the prisoners they did not visit, and the King says that what they did not do for the least of these, they did not do for him (Matthew 25:41–46). Sins of omission are never mere gaps. The good left undone was good owed to Christ, in the person he set in our path.

He gave himself for our tomorrows. Only one man never failed to do the good he knew. Jesus always knew his Father’s will, and did all of it: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). He bore our sins of omission as well as our sins of commission, the good we left undone along with the evil we did, and his perfect doing is counted as ours. He did not boast about tomorrow; he gave himself for our tomorrows, and rose to make them his.

In everyday life. What good thing do you know you should do but have been putting off? Do it today, in the strength of the Spirit who now lives in you; if it is too big for today, take the first step today.

There is so much good I could do. Am I sinning all the time by not doing it? No. James is not saying you must do every good thing in the world, which no one can. He means the specific good God puts in front of you and that you know you ought to do: the call you should make, the apology you owe, the duty of your own calling. God gives each of us particular responsibilities and limits; even Jesus did not heal everyone in Israel. Do what he has clearly put in your path, and trust him with the rest. This verse should lead to obedience, not to paralysis.

What about the good I failed to do in the past? Bring it to Christ. Sins of omission are forgiven like any other sin through his blood (1 John 1:9). Where you can still put something right, do it; where you cannot, leave it with him. Then let this verse shape tomorrow rather than haunt yesterday. The warning is meant not to load you with guilt but to move you to act now, while it is still today.

You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask.<sup>3</sup>You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.<sup>4</sup>You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.<sup>5</sup>Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us”?<sup>6</sup>But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”<sup>7</sup>Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.<sup>8</sup>Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.<sup>9</sup>Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.<sup>10</sup>Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.<sup>11</sup>Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks evil against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge.<sup>12</sup>There is only one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?<sup>13</sup>Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”—<sup>14</sup>yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring.
