keyVerse.quote: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
keyVerse.note: After five verses of diagnosis, this is the hinge of the chapter: the God whose demand is total gives grace greater than our worst betrayal. The quotation from Proverbs 3:34 names the one condition, a humble heart, and the ten commands that follow (vv. 7–10) show what it is to come to him low. Every other line of the chapter, from the quarrels to the boast about tomorrow, is a form of the pride God opposes.

4.reflection:
James says our quarrels come from “your passions are at war within you” (v. 1). Think of a recent argument, at home, at work or in church. What did you really want underneath it, and what would it have looked like to ask God for it instead of fighting for it?

James calls friendship with the world spiritual adultery (v. 4). If worldliness is about the heart’s loyalty more than particular things, where do you see it in your own life or in this church? What would the question “What would I be most devastated to lose?” reveal?

“But he gives more grace” (v. 6). Why does God’s grace reach the humble and not the proud? How do the commands of verses 7–10 help us to come to him low, and which of them do you find hardest?

Verses 11–17 describe two ways of taking God’s place: judging a brother and boasting about tomorrow. Which is the greater temptation for you, and what difference would it make this week to say, and mean, “If the Lord wills”?

5.title: Patient Until He Comes: Wealth, Endurance, and Prayer
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 ended with traders planning their year as if tomorrow were theirs, and with the sin of good left undone (4:13–17). Chapter 5 turns the same “Come now” on rich landowners, then turns tenderly to the suffering church and brings the letter to a close.

The message. The Lord is coming, and his coming means opposite things for oppressor and oppressed. For those who hoard and cheat it is ruin: their wealth is already rotting, and the cries of the men they robbed have reached him. For his suffering people it is hope. So wait for him without revenge or grumbling, let your plain word be true, bring every condition of life to God in prayer, and go after the brother who wanders.

Why it was said. James’s readers were poor and hard-pressed, cheated of wages and dragged into court by the rich (2:6; see the introduction), and tempted to strike back, to turn on one another, to doubt that God saw, or to stop praying. James answers: God sees, he is near, and meanwhile he hears.

How the chapter makes its case. First a prophet’s woe, which the church overhears (vv. 1–6): the oppressors’ riches have rotted and will testify against them, the withheld wages cry out to the Lord of hosts, and their luxury is fattening them for slaughter. “Therefore” the church is to wait like a farmer for the rains, steady in heart, not grumbling, taking heart from the prophets and Job (vv. 7–11), and speaking so truthfully that no oath is needed (v. 12). Then James turns the whole of life into prayer: the suffering pray, the cheerful sing, the sick call the elders, believers confess to one another, and Elijah, a man like us, shows what such prayer can do (vv. 13–18). The letter ends, without a greeting, on one believer going after another (vv. 19–20).

Where it leads. The righteous man who does not resist (v. 6) reminds us of the Righteous One who stood silent before a rigged court. The Lord for whom the farmer waits is the Judge already at the door (vv. 7–9). The compassion Job glimpsed walked through Galilee and went to the cross (v. 11). And the Son who took a nature like ours always lives to pray for his people, and as the Good Shepherd goes after every wanderer until he finds him (vv. 17–20).

For us. Ask how you hold your money. Wait for Christ with a steady heart, not a bitter one. Take your trouble, joy, sickness and sin to God and to one another. And go after one person who has drifted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wealth gained by injustice and hoarded in luxury is already under God’s judgment, for the Lord of hosts has heard the cries of those it wronged. James speaks to the rich oppressors as the prophets spoke to the nations, while the church overhears. Their riches have rotted, and the rust will testify against them (vv. 1–3). The cheated harvesters have been heard, and the luxury bought with their wages is fattening its owners for a day of slaughter (vv. 4–5). They have condemned and killed the righteous, who could not resist (v. 6). For the oppressed it is the assurance that God sees and will act.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rust That Testifies

Hoarded wealth will testify against those who kept back the wages of their labourers. The cries of the harvesters have reached the Lord of hosts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A day-labourer's withheld wage meant a family without supper.

Now: Comfort bought by someone else's hunger is not a blessing but fattening for a day of slaughter.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure in the last days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wealth hoarded while others go without is already rotting, and at the judgment its rust will testify against its owners.

Come now, you rich. The same abrupt summons as in 4:13, now to the rich, probably wealthy unbelievers who oppressed the poor believers (2:6–7). James addresses them as the prophets addressed the nations while God’s people listened (Isaiah 13; Amos 4:1).

Weep and howl. Howl is the shriek of those under God’s judgment (Isaiah 13:6; 15:3). The miseries are still coming, but are so certain that James tells the rich to weep now.

Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Three kinds of wealth, each longer-lasting than the one before, and all have failed: food, clothing, metal. Rot is what happens to stored grain and produce, like the rich fool’s barns (Luke 12:18–20). Fine clothing was a major form of savings in that world, and it takes no thief to lose it: a moth will do. “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy” (Matthew 6:19–20).

Your gold and silver have corroded. Gold does not corrode, and James knows it. He makes his point by overstatement: even the one asset that cannot decay has decayed. Nothing they own has survived.

Evidence against you. Testimony for the prosecution. Metal that is spent does not corrode; this corroded because it was hoarded while the men who earned it went hungry. And the corrosion that consumed the treasure “will eat your flesh like fire”: the wealth they trusted becomes the instrument of their judgment.

In the last days. The final age before judgment, which began with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). They were piling up wealth just when it could do them least good, like a man buying property in a town he knows is to be flooded.

Treasure in heaven. James sharpens Jesus’ own woe to the rich (Luke 6:24). But when a rich man asked about eternal life, Jesus looked at him, loved him, and offered him treasure in heaven if he would give to the poor and follow him (Mark 10:21). The hoarders were storing up the one kind of treasure that perishes, in the very age when the other kind was being offered. And the Judge who will call them to account emptied himself of every treasure: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). He had nowhere to lay his head. He is our treasure, and he does not rust.

What it does not mean. Not that all wealth is evil: Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly. James condemns hoarding, oppression, fraud and self-indulgence.

If I am comfortably off, is this passage about me? Its first target is the unbelieving rich, but it searches anyone with more than they need, which includes most readers in the West. It asks not how much you have, but how you got it, whether you are hoarding it, and whether anyone has gone without because of you. The rich are to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). Wealth held open-handed is a tool for the kingdom; wealth clutched is a witness for the prosecution.

How do I know if I am hoarding rather than saving wisely? Saving for real needs, a home, your children, old age, emergencies, is wise and biblical (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). Hoarding keeps far beyond need, out of fear or love of money, while needs around you go unmet. Some honest tests: Do I give generously and regularly, or only from what is left over? Does my security rest in my savings or in God? Is there a need in front of me that I could meet and am refusing to? Talk it through with a wise believer; money is where we deceive ourselves most easily.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wages the rich withheld cry out to God, and he has heard: the luxury those wages bought is fattening its owners for judgment.

Wages kept back by fraud. The law was explicit: a hired man was to be paid before sunset, because he is poor and counts on it (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). A day-labourer had no savings; to withhold his wage overnight meant a family going without supper. So the wages themselves cry out, and so do the men, as Abel’s blood cried to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

The Lord of hosts. The LORD of armies, who defends the oppressed (Isaiah 5:9). The defrauded workers have no advocate and no standing, yet their case has been heard by the commander of heaven’s armies (Exodus 3:7). Malachi had used the title in this very connection: the LORD of hosts would be a swift witness against those who oppress the hired worker in his wages (Malachi 3:5).

Luxury, and a day of slaughter. Soft living and wanton pleasure, like the rich man who feasted every day while Lazarus lay at his gate (Luke 16:19): comfort at one table bought by hunger at another. Like cattle fattened for the slaughter (Jeremiah 12:3), they have stuffed themselves without knowing what the day is for. They took their prosperity as God’s favour; it was fattening them for judgment.

Condemned and murdered. “Condemned” is a courtroom word: the courts were used against a man who could not afford to defend himself (2:6), and for a day-labourer that could mean death. “The righteous person” means the innocent poor in general, and perhaps also points to Jesus, the Righteous One (Acts 3:14; 7:52).

He does not resist you. There was never a contest: the righteous poor are helpless, or choose not to retaliate (Matthew 5:39). Yet the powerless man’s silence is not the end of the matter.

The Righteous One. Jesus too did not resist those who condemned him. He stood silent before a rigged court, was condemned by the powerful, and in his silence bore the sins of oppressors and oppressed alike. His blood cries out like Abel’s, but it “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24): not vengeance, but forgiveness for all who come to him.

Good news to the poor. The Lord who hears the harvesters did more than hear. In Jesus he came among working people as the carpenter of Nazareth (Mark 6:3), announcing good news to the poor and liberty for the oppressed (Luke 4:18). The defrauded worker has an advocate who once worked with his own hands.

What does this mean for me as an employer, a customer or a manager? Pay people fairly and on time, and do not use your power to squeeze those who cannot push back: the cleaner, the builder, the freelancer whose invoice sits unpaid for months. “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1). As a customer, care, as far as you reasonably can, whether the cheapness of what you buy depends on someone else’s exploitation.

Is God on the side of the poor? God is on the side of justice, and Scripture repeatedly shows him hearing the cry of the poor, the widow and the oppressed when no one else does (Psalm 146:7–9). The poor are not saved by being poor, nor the rich condemned by being rich; salvation is by grace through faith in Christ for all. But the oppressed have a Judge, and the church should share his heart, speaking up for the voiceless and refusing to flatter the powerful.

If God hears the cry, why does he let the cheating go on so long? The psalmist asked it too, until he went into the sanctuary of God and saw their end (Psalm 73:16–17). The cries have already reached the Lord’s ears, and the account is kept down to the last unpaid wage. The delay is not deafness but patience, not wishing that any should perish, the oppressor included (2 Peter 3:9). So the wronged can wait without despair, and the wrongdoer still has time to repent and repay, as Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8).

In everyday life. Check this week whether there is any bill, wage or debt you have been sitting on, and pay it. If you are the one defrauded, bring your cry to the Lord of hosts, plainly and in detail.

Uncertain wording. “In a day of slaughter” is literally “in”, not “for”, such a day. Most take it of the coming judgment; some of the present, the rich feasting while the poor are destroyed, like soldiers gorging after a battle. The first fits “the last days” of verse 3 better. And since Greek has no question marks, “He does not resist you” could be a question, “Does he not resist you?”, with God as the one who opposes them (4:6). The plain statement, as in the ESV, is more natural; on either reading the oppressor does not have the last word.
verseByVerse.note: The Law required day-labourers to be paid the same day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–20 — Patience, Prayer, and Going After the Wanderer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the Lord is coming, his people can wait without revenge and bring every part of life to God in prayer. Like a farmer waiting for the rains they are to steady their hearts (vv. 7–8), stop grumbling at one another with the Judge at the door (v. 9), and take heart from the prophets and from Job, whose story showed the Lord compassionate and merciful (vv. 10–11). Their plain word is to be true (v. 12). In suffering, gladness and sickness they turn to God, the sick calling for the elders (vv. 13–15); they confess their sins and pray for one another, as ordinary as Elijah and as surely heard (vv. 16–18). And the letter ends by sending them after the one who wanders (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prayer of Faith

Be patient as the farmer waits for the rains, because the Lord is coming. Pray in every condition; the prayer of faith is prayer submitted to God's will, and Elijah was a man like us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Pressed from outside, the congregation was grumbling against one another.

Now: The letter ends by sending ordinary believers after the one who has wandered.

verseByVerse.quote: Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains. You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the Lord is coming to put every wrong right, his people can wait for him without striking back, with hearts made firm, as a farmer waits for the rain.

Be patient, therefore. James turns back to the congregation, and his tone softens. “Therefore”: because God will judge the oppressors. Patience (makrothymia) is being long-tempered, slow to burn: the patience that does not hit back. Having heard their oppressors denounced, they might take matters into their own hands; James says, wait for the King to act.

The coming of the Lord is at hand. Coming (parousia) was the word for a king’s official visit (1 Thessalonians 4:15). And it is “at hand”: he has drawn near and is near now (Romans 13:11–12; Philippians 4:5). James gives no date, but the nearness turns patience into hope.

The farmer waits. In Israel the early rain came in autumn and the late rain in spring (Deuteronomy 11:14; Joel 2:23), with months between in which nothing could be done. The farmer has ploughed and sown, and he will reap, but no activity in the world brings the harvest forward by a day. It is certain, and it comes in its time.

Establish your hearts. Make them firm. To wait well, the heart must be steady, and it is God who establishes us in Christ, with his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee (2 Corinthians 1:21–22).

The harvest is Christ himself. The one who came first in weakness, to a manger and a cross, will come again in glory, and every eye will see him. He will judge every wrong, comfort every mourner and raise his people from the dust. The farmer’s waiting ends in harvest, and the harvest is Christ himself and all who belong to him. “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

How do I establish my heart while I wait? A heart is made firm the way a fence post is: by being driven into something that does not move. Tell yourself, in so many words, that Christ is coming and will put right what is wrong. Carry one promise of his coming (John 14:3) through the day. Pray your impatience to him plainly, rather than letting it harden into bitterness against the people nearest you (v. 9). Wait with his people, who at the Lord’s Table proclaim his death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). And remember who does the establishing. Christ himself is waiting at the Father’s right hand until his enemies are made a footstool for his feet (Hebrews 10:12–13), and he holds you while he waits. The steadiness is his before it is yours.

What will actually happen when he comes? One visible, glorious return at the end of this age, seen by all (Acts 1:11; Revelation 1:7). Many Christians expect a secret rapture of the church before a time of tribulation, and hold it out of real love for his appearing; this commentary reads the passages differently, because the coming in 1 Thessalonians 4 is loud and public, with a cry of command and the trumpet of God, and the New Testament speaks of one return, not two. The dead will be raised, living believers changed and caught up to meet him, and he will judge the living and the dead (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52; Matthew 25:31–46). Then come eternal punishment and eternal life, and a new heaven and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13).

If I am suffering injustice now, does patience mean I should not seek justice? No. Patience forbids revenge and bitterness, not lawful justice. Paul insisted on his rights as a Roman citizen and appealed to Caesar (Acts 16:37; 25:11). If you are wronged, you may use proper means: the courts, the police, the employment tribunal, the church’s elders. If you are being abused, get to safety and report it. What James forbids is taking vengeance into your own hands, and the despair that thinks God has forgotten. Leave the final reckoning to the Lord, who will repay (Romans 12:19).

Where Christians differ: was James wrong about the nearness of Christ’s return, since two thousand years have passed? Critics argue that the early church expected Jesus to return within their lifetime and was mistaken. This commentary’s view: near in the New Testament describes the whole age since Christ’s resurrection. His return is the next great event in God’s plan: no date is given, and every generation must live ready (Revelation 22:7). Paul says that a final rebellion and the man of lawlessness will come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so near does not mean that no prophecy remains; but these are not a timetable to calculate, for the mystery of lawlessness is already at work (2 Thessalonians 2:7), and the day will still come like a thief on those who are not watching (1 Thessalonians 5:2–4). With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day; the delay is his patience, giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:8–9).
verseByVerse.note: In Israel the early rain came in autumn, at sowing, and the late rain in spring, before harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pressure from outside must not turn believers against one another, for the Judge who will right their wrongs is near enough to hear their muttering.

Do not grumble. To grumble is to groan or sigh: not open quarrelling but muttering, the remark to one person about another, like Israel in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:10). People pressed from outside who cannot push back take it out on those nearest them, as families do under financial strain.

So that you may not be judged. To grumble about someone is to pass sentence on him in private (4:11–12), and the man who sets himself up as judge will be judged himself (Matthew 7:1).

The Judge is standing at the door. The Judge is Christ (Acts 10:42), about to enter (Matthew 24:33). It is a comfort: the oppressed are told their Judge has arrived. And in the same breath a warning: he is at the door of their room too, about to walk in on the muttering.

The Judge who knocks. The Judge at the door is the Saviour who knocks: if anyone opens the door, “I will come in to him and eat with him” (Revelation 3:20). He bore with the grumbling of Israel for forty years, and of his disciples through his ministry. His patience with us is the reason we can be patient with one another.

What is the difference between grumbling and lament? Lament takes the complaint to God; grumbling takes it to everyone except God and the person concerned. Lament is honest about pain and ends in trust: “How long, O LORD?” but “I have trusted in your steadfast love” (Psalm 13:1, 5). Lament seeks God’s help; grumbling seeks allies. If you have a real grievance against a brother, go to him (Matthew 18:15). If you have a grief you cannot fix, take it to God. Either way, stop muttering.

verseByVerse.quote: As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophets and Job show that enduring under suffering is the way of blessing, and Job’s story shows how it ends: the Lord is compassionate and merciful.

Take the prophets. Prophets like Jeremiah suffered rejection, imprisonment and death (Matthew 5:12; Hebrews 11:32–38), not despite their faithfulness but because they spoke in the Lord’s name. A congregation oppressed for its faith stands in their line, not outside it.

Those blessed who remained steadfast. James goes back to hypomonē, the steadfast endurance of chapter 1, and “blessed” repeats 1:12. The letter ends where it began.

The steadfastness of Job. Job was not patient in the sense the word has acquired in English. He protested at length and told God he had a case to argue. What he did was not let go of God (Job 1:21), which is what hypomonē means: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15); “I know that my Redeemer lives” (Job 19:25). Endurance is not silence but holding on.

The purpose of the Lord. The outcome (telos): how it turned out. God restored Job and revealed himself to him (Job 42:10–17). Job could not see it from inside; the reader of the book can.

Compassionate and merciful. A remarkable conclusion from a book that never explains Job’s suffering. James does not say the Lord explained himself, but that the end of the story showed what he is like, as he described himself at Sinai: “a God merciful and gracious” (Exodus 34:6). James’s rare word for compassionate (polysplanchnos) is built on the word for the inward parts, and the Gospels use its verb again and again of Jesus, who had compassion on the harassed crowds and on the widow of Nain behind her son’s bier (Matthew 9:36; Luke 7:13).

Compassion with a face. What Job glimpsed at the end of his book, the reader of the Gospels can watch walking through Galilee, and finally see at a cross and an empty tomb.

Is it all right to complain to God the way Job did? Yes, if you complain to him and not away from him. The Psalms are full of honest complaint, given to teach us how to pray in the dark. Job’s friends, with their tidy explanations, were rebuked; Job, who wrestled honestly, was vindicated (Job 42:7). What God corrected in Job was the edge of accusation, the demand that God answer to him (Job 38–40). So pour out your heart, and then, like Job, put your hand over your mouth before his majesty and keep trusting.

Will God give me back what I lost, as he did for Job? He often restores in some measure, but he has not promised to repay every loss here. The children Job buried were not replaced by the new ones, but Job looked for a Redeemer who would stand on the earth at the last. For those in Christ nothing is finally lost: our telos is resurrection, reunion and a world made new.

In everyday life. If someone you know is suffering, do not be Job’s friends. Sit with them, listen, weep with them, and resist the urge to explain.

Uncertain wording. “The purpose of the Lord” translates to telos kyriou, literally “the end of the Lord”. Most take it as the outcome the Lord brought about in Job’s story (Job 42:10–17). Some older interpreters took it of the Lord Jesus’ own end, his death and resurrection, but nothing in the sentence points away from Job, and James at once says what that end showed: “how the Lord is compassionate and merciful”.

verseByVerse.quote: But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians should be so truthful that their plain yes and no need no oath to prop them up.

But above all, do not swear. “Above all” most likely marks a final, weighty point; it may come here because people under suffering make rash oaths. It echoes Jesus almost word for word (Matthew 5:33–37).

By heaven or by earth. The habit of propping up ordinary speech with oaths by heaven, by earth, by the temple. A graded system grew up in which some oaths bound and others were escape routes (Matthew 23:16–22): a device for deceiving while appearing truthful. Jesus and James reject the game, for all speech is spoken before God, and a man who must swear to be believed has admitted that his ordinary word is not reliable.

So that you may not fall under condemnation. The warning sounds heavier than the subject deserves, and that is the point: God is not deceived by the gradations.

Truly, I say to you. Jesus never swore by heaven or by the temple. He began his weightiest sayings with “Truly, I say to you” (in his own language, “Amen”), and no oath propped them up, because he is the truth (John 14:6). The plain yes James asks of us is learned from him.

Does this forbid all oaths, even in court or at a wedding? No (see the box at the end of this note). James forbids casual swearing; wedding vows and the solemn promises of church membership or ordination are lawful vows made before God, and should be kept.

What about phrases like I swear, honestly, or to be honest with you? They are the modern version of the same habit. If you need to say honestly, what does that imply about the rest of what you say? Most are thoughtless habits rather than wicked oaths, but James invites us to drop the props, and the exaggerations (always, never, literally, everyone), and let plain words carry the weight.

In everyday life. Every promise of God is Yes in Christ, and his truthfulness is counted as yours even where your word has failed. Keep every promise you make this week, including the small ones; if you cannot keep one, say so honestly and early.

Where Christians differ: are all oaths forbidden? Some, such as Quakers and many Anabaptists, refuse any oath, even in court, out of a sincere wish to obey Jesus’ words to the letter. This commentary’s view: James and Jesus forbid casual, frivolous and evasive oaths in everyday speech, and oaths used to manipulate, not solemn, lawful oaths required by proper authority, as in court. God himself swore oaths (Hebrews 6:13–18); Jesus answered under oath before the high priest (Matthew 26:63–64); Paul called God as witness (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23). The Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession rightly regard lawful oaths as part of religious worship (Westminster 22.1; 1689 23.1). The heart of the command is simple, consistent truthfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every condition of life is to be taken to God: trouble in prayer, gladness in praise.

Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Three questions in quick succession, the first two answered in a single word in the Greek, turn every mood of the Christian life into prayer or praise. Suffering (kakopathei) is hardship of any kind, the same root as the suffering of the prophets in verse 10. The response is not grumbling (v. 9), swearing (v. 12) or a search for the reason, but prayer (proseuchesthō, keep praying). The patience of verses 7–11 prays while it waits, and the letter comes full circle: it opened with trials and asking God in faith (1:2–8), and closes with sickness and the prayer of faith (5:15).

Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise. The half we habitually neglect. Cheerful (euthymei) is in good spirits; sing praise (psalletō) is to sing psalms, sing with music (Ephesians 5:19). Trouble goes up as prayer, joy as song, and between them they cover every day anybody has. A man who prays only when suffering has a relationship with his own need rather than with God. James is not against any emotion, only against keeping every emotion to oneself.

Through one name. Both the groan and the song go up by the same way: we ask the Father in Jesus’ name (John 16:23–24). The sufferer need not compose himself first, nor the glad man justify his gladness.

He wept and sang before us. The Son himself prayed with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7), and sang a hymn with his disciples on the night he was betrayed (Matthew 26:30). Now he leads the praise of his people: “in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (Hebrews 2:12). Whether we weep or laugh, we never come to God alone.

What if I am neither suffering nor cheerful, just flat and numb? Then bring the numbness. The Psalms include prayers from people who felt nothing but distance (Psalm 88); read one aloud and let its words carry you when your own are gone. Keep the habits of prayer and worship going even when they feel mechanical, like a fire laid, ready to catch. And if the flatness persists, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, and see your doctor for a check-up; it may be depression, which needs care, not condemnation.

I cannot sing well. Does that matter? Not at all. God is listening for hearts, not quality. Singing is commanded for all God’s people, not just the musical (Psalm 100:1–2), and the joyful noise counts. Sing in the car, hum while you work, or read a psalm of praise aloud.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A seriously ill believer should call for the elders to pray over him in the Lord’s name, and the Lord hears that prayer: he raises up the sick and forgives the sinner.

Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church. Sick (asthenei) is weak, ill, probably seriously ill, since the elders come to him rather than he to them. He is the one who calls, and he calls the elders, plural: the ordinary appointed leaders of the local church. Prayer for the sick is not left to individuals with special gifts; it is part of the elders’ ordinary pastoral care.

Anointing him with oil. They pray over him, and the anointing serves the praying. Oil was both medicine (Luke 10:34) and a sign of setting someone apart for God (1 Samuel 16:13); the Twelve also anointed the sick (Mark 6:13). Whichever it chiefly is, the oil is not what matters most. The praying is, done in the name of the Lord.

The prayer of faith will save the one who is sick. The power is not in the oil or the elders but in God. Save means rescue, heal, restore: here chiefly physical healing, though it can include more. Read alone, this seems to promise that every believing prayer heals, and every Christian knows it does not. Asking can be answered no (4:3), and Paul was not always healed or able to heal (2 Timothy 4:20). The prayer of faith is not confidence worked up: that would make the sick man’s illness his own fault, the very cruelty this verse has often been used to inflict. It is prayer offered in submission to God’s will. And “save” and “raise up” reach beyond recovery: every believer will finally be raised up at the resurrection, whether or not this illness ends.

If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven. The “if” is careful and merciful. Not all sickness is caused by sin (John 9:2–3), but some is (1 Corinthians 11:30), and then confession and prayer bring forgiveness. James allows that sin may be involved and refuses to assume it, the balance Job’s friends failed to keep.

The Lord at the bedside. In the Gospels the sick were carried to Jesus, and he healed them with a word or a touch (Mark 1:32–34). He is ascended now, but he is not a different Lord. The elders bring the sick man to him in prayer, and his compassion has not cooled (Hebrews 13:8), even when his answer is not the one we asked for.

Should churches still anoint with oil? Elders may still pray over the sick and anoint them, and this does not oppose medicine: Christians should use doctors and pray.

We prayed, and my loved one died. Was our faith too weak? No. The death of someone you prayed for is not proof that you lacked faith or that God did not hear. Faith is not a force that obliges God but trust in his wisdom and love, and sometimes his answer is to take his child home. For the believer, death is the final healing: the Lord raised them up, not from the sickbed but into his presence, where there is no more pain (Revelation 21:4). Your prayers were not wasted; they were part of carrying your loved one to the Lord. Grieve freely, as one who has hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and do not let anyone load you with guilt this verse never imposed.

How do I actually call for the elders? Simply ask. Tell your pastor or one of the elders that you are seriously ill, and ask them to come and pray with you. They may read Scripture, ask whether there is anything you want to confess, pray for healing and for God’s will, and perhaps anoint you with a little oil on the forehead: not a ritual to perform correctly but the church’s care. Many believers never ask because they do not want to be a bother. James says: call them.

Where Christians differ: is this a sacrament of last rites, or a promise of guaranteed healing? Roman Catholic teaching sees this as the sacrament of the anointing of the sick (formerly extreme unction, given to the dying). Some teachers in the healing and prosperity movements take it as a guarantee that God always heals in response to faith. This commentary’s view: James describes prayer aimed at recovery, not preparation for death, so it is not last rites; and Christ commanded his church to keep only two sacraments, or ordinances: baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Nor is it an unconditional guarantee: God answers according to his will (1 John 5:14), and even Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20) and was not healed of his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). The passage gives a continuing pattern for church life: elders praying in faith for the sick, using oil as a sign if they choose, trusting God to heal as he wills. This is distinct from the apostolic sign gifts of healing, which this commentary holds have ceased: they were signs confirming the apostles’ message while the New Testament was being given (Acts 2:43; 2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and it is telling that James sends the sick man to the elders, not to a healer. God still heals in answer to prayer. Many faithful Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe such gifts continue and pray for the sick with real love and faith; we differ as brothers, and on both views the sick are brought to the same compassionate Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Oil was used as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are to bring their sins into the open with one another and pray for one another, because God works powerfully through the prayers of ordinary forgiven people.

Confess your sins to one another. Since sin may lie behind trouble, deal with it in the open. James means neither confession to a priest nor to God only, but ordinary Christians telling each other the truth about themselves, and most of us avoid it. Yet sin kept private grows in the dark, fed by the fear of exposure; once a man has told somebody, the secrecy that protected it is gone. “When I kept silent, my bones wasted away” (Psalm 32:3–5).

Pray for one another, that you may be healed. Confession alone leaves a person exposed, so James joins it to intercession, for healing of body, soul and community (Hebrews 12:13). The righteous person whose prayer has such power is not a sinless super-saint, or the verse would discourage the very people it was written for, but a believer whose sins are confessed and forgiven; James’s example, Elijah, was made of the same stuff as we are. Such prayer is not power kept in store but power at work as it is prayed (see the box at the end of this note).

Confessed under the cross. Confession between believers is safe only because Christ carried our sins to the cross: “By his wounds you have been healed,” Peter says, using James’s word for healing (1 Peter 2:24). So the brother who hears a confession does not absolve and need not be shocked; he points to a sin already carried, and prays. For those in Christ there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1): the light that floods the place where sin hid does not condemn.

We disclose everything except our sins. People today tell the world about their anxieties, diagnoses and break-ups, often bravely, yet confession in James’s sense has almost disappeared. We share our wounds and our quirks, and keep back our wrongs. If my worth rests on my image, admitting real sin is a small death, so the self-revealing culture is also a deeply hidden one. Dietrich Bonhoeffer argued in Life Together that a church can be lonely in exactly this way: everyone is devout, so no one is permitted to be a sinner, and each hides his sin from the rest. The gospel breaks the deadlock: you can afford to be known as a sinner only when you are already accepted as one, and in Christ you are. The worst thing about you has been seen, judged and carried. What is left to protect?

What it does not mean. Not that every sin must be confessed publicly to the whole church. Wisdom guides what to confess and to whom: a sin against a person to that person; private struggles to a trusted friend or elder.

Whom should I confess to, and how? Choose a mature, trustworthy believer of the same sex, or an elder: someone who will keep confidence, point you to Christ, pray for you and help you fight. Be specific; “I have been struggling” is not confession. Say what you did. Then ask them to pray, there and then if possible, and to ask you about it again. You are confessing to a fellow sinner, not to a judge.

What if the person I confess to betrays my trust? It is a real risk, which is why you should choose carefully, and a believer who gossips about a confession has sinned seriously. But do not let the fear stop you entirely; most Christians trusted with a confession are humbled and honoured, and keep it. Start small, with someone you have good reason to trust. And if a confession involves a crime, particularly harm to a child or a vulnerable person, it must not be kept secret; protecting the vulnerable comes before confidentiality.

In everyday life. Be the kind of person others can confess to: unshockable, discreet, quick to pray and quick to point to Christ.

Where Christians differ: is confession to a priest required? Roman Catholic teaching requires confession of serious sins to a priest for absolution. This commentary’s view: James commands confession to one another, among all believers, not to a priestly class. Forgiveness comes from God through Christ, our only mediator (1 Timothy 2:5; 1 John 1:9). Confessing to a trusted believer or elder is a valuable means of grace, accountability and healing, but it is not a sacrament, and no human being stands between the believer and God.

Uncertain wording. “As it is working” translates a single Greek participle (energoumenē) whose exact force is uncertain. It may mean “in its working”, prayer as power actively at work, or, read as passive, “when it is made effective”, that is, by God. Either way the power belongs to God, and it is at work as believers pray.

verseByVerse.quote: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth. Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah was an ordinary man whose earnest prayers God answered, so the prayers of ordinary believers are heard too.

A nature like ours. Elijah is among the most spectacular prophets: fire from heaven on Carmel, ravens that fed him, a chariot of fire. He is exactly the man a discouraged congregation would point to as proof that prayer works for other people, and James removes the objection at once: he had the same nature as we have. Right after one of the most dramatic answers to prayer in the Old Testament, he sat under a broom tree and asked God to let him die (1 Kings 19:3–4). The God who answered that depressed prophet, with bread and water and then a low whisper, is the God who hears us.

He prayed fervently. Literally “he prayed with prayer”, a Hebrew idiom for earnestness. 1 Kings 17:1 records his announcement of the drought; James understands it to have rested on prayer. The drought was God’s judgment on Ahab’s idolatry (Deuteronomy 11:16–17).

Three years and six months. Jesus gives the same figure (Luke 4:25). 1 Kings 18:1 says the word came “in the third year”, probably counting from Elijah’s stay at Zarephath.

He prayed again. On Carmel Elijah bowed with his face between his knees and sent his servant to look seven times before the rain came (1 Kings 18:41–45), bringing back the farmer of verse 7.

The righteous man who is always heard. The Son of God also took a nature like ours (Hebrews 2:17), and at Lazarus’s tomb he said he knew the Father always hears him (John 11:41–42). He always lives to intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25). So the prayers of weak believers, despairing under their own broom trees, are joined to the intercession of a righteous man who is never refused.

Can I pray for things like rain, or a job, or a parking space? Yes. Nothing that concerns you is too small for your Father, who numbers the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30). But hold every request with an open hand: “your will be done”. What separates Elijah’s prayer from a superstitious one is not the size of the request but its submission: he prayed in line with what God had said, and for God’s name to be honoured.

What does fervent prayer look like for an ordinary person? Not necessarily long or loud, but earnest and persistent, like Elijah sending his servant to look seven times: specific requests rather than vague wishes, coming back day after day, grounded in God’s promises. It might be one honest sentence prayed every morning for a wayward child for twenty years. God is not impressed by eloquence; he hears the cry of his children.

In everyday life. Choose one thing you know is in line with God’s will, such as the salvation of a friend, and pray for it earnestly every day, looking at the horizon, like Elijah’s servant, for the small cloud.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah’s prayers are implied in 1 Kings; Jesus also gives the drought’s length as three and a half years.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To go after a believer who has drifted from the truth is the greatest kindness one Christian can show another, for God uses it to rescue him from death and to cover his sins.

If anyone among you wanders from the truth. The verb is to be led astray, the root of our word planet, the wandering star. It is drift, not a decision; nobody announces that they are leaving.

Someone brings him back. That someone is very ordinary: not the elders or an office, but anyone who notices and goes after him (Galatians 6:1). The letter ends without benediction or greetings, on somebody else’s soul. James has insisted that real faith shows in deeds, and he ends with the most concrete act of love available to an ordinary Christian: noticing that someone has stopped coming, and going to find out why.

Save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins. Nothing higher could be said of one Christian going after another (Romans 6:23). God saves, but he uses believers as his instruments. The phrase about covering echoes Proverbs 10:12 (also 1 Peter 4:8), and the covering is God’s work: the wanderer’s sins are forgiven when he returns.

Turned again. The word for bringing back is the one Jesus used to Peter: “when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Peter wandered as far as a disciple can, and the risen Lord went after him by the lake, three questions for three denials (John 21:15–17). The Son of Man still seeks the lost (Luke 19:10), through the ordinary believer who knocks on a wanderer’s door.

Over the mountains and into the dark. That is what God is like. “All we like sheep have gone astray” (Isaiah 53:6), and the Good Shepherd left the ninety-nine and came after us, over the mountains and into the dark, until he found us and laid us on his shoulders rejoicing. He did not merely cover a multitude of sins; he bore them in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24–25). Every time one believer goes after another, it is the Shepherd’s love walking out of the door again.

Can a true believer wander so far as to be lost? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer can finally fall away, read the verse so, out of a serious concern for holiness. The more likely reading is that the wanderer is either a believer whom God restores through the loving pursuit of others, or a professing member whose wandering would have shown that his faith was never real. Either way, the person who brings him back is God’s means of keeping him, which is why we must not leave wanderers alone.

How do I approach someone who has drifted away? Go personally, not with a programme. Begin with friendship, not a lecture: a message, a coffee, an invitation to a meal. Tell them they are missed, and mean it. Listen more than you speak; there may be hurt, doubt, sin or simply busyness behind the drift. When the time is right, be honest, gently, about your concern for their soul. Pray before and after, keep watch on yourself (Galatians 6:1), and do not give up after one attempt. The shepherd went after the one sheep until he found it (Luke 15:4).

What if they do not want to come back? Then you have still done what love requires, and the result belongs to God. Keep praying, keep the door open, and keep being their friend if they will let you, without pretending that all is well. Some come back after many years, remembering the one who did not give up on them. If there is serious unrepentant sin, the elders may need to be involved (Matthew 18:15–17), always aiming at restoration. You cannot force anyone home, but you can make sure they know the way back is open, and that someone is watching for them.

Uncertain wording. The Greek says only that whoever brings back a sinner “will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins”, without naming whose soul or whose sins. Grammatically either could be the restorer’s, and some have taken them so. But the one in danger of death is the wanderer, and the sins are those of his wandering. The restorer is God’s instrument, not a man earning his own pardon.

keyVerse.quote: You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge between the chapter’s two halves. The coming of the Lord that spells ruin for the oppressors (vv. 1–6) is the hope that steadies his suffering people. Everything that follows, from refusing to grumble to praying for the sick and going after the wanderer, is what an established heart does while it waits.

5.reflection:
James tells the rich that their hoarded wealth “will be evidence against you” (v. 3). If your spending, saving and giving were read out as evidence, what would they say about where your treasure is? What is one way you could hold what you have more open-handedly?

“Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand” (v. 8). What are you waiting for that God has not yet given? How does the certainty of Christ’s return change the way you wait, and the way you speak about other people while you wait (v. 9)?

Verses 13–16 send every condition of life to God: suffering to prayer, gladness to praise, sickness to the elders, sin to confession. Which of these do you find hardest, and why? What would help this church become a place where people ask for prayer and confess their sins to one another?

The letter ends with someone going after a wanderer (vv. 19–20). Is there someone you know who has drifted from Christ or from church? What might it look like to go after them this week, and how does the Good Shepherd’s pursuit of you shape the way you go?
